`slopvac` lints prose and source comments. Its rules cover AI writing patterns
and general prose quality, including documentation discipline and
technical-writing constraints. Use it on AI-generated documentation, PR
descriptions, Markdown, and comments in supported source files such as TSX and
JSX. Comment mode checks comments, not code or strings.

Coding agents use the CLI to inspect findings and apply fixes. The same checks
can run in pre-commit or CI for automated validation.

Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) and use
Python 3.11 or later. **[Vale](https://vale.sh) 3.18 or later is required
for a complete lint run.** Vale executes most deterministic rules and must be
available on `PATH`. Slopvac checks the Vale version before compiling rules.
Without Vale, lint exits 2 (incomplete) instead of 0 (pass).
With Homebrew, install Vale and check the installed version:

Other platforms can use the [Vale installation instructions](https://vale.sh).
Contributors can run `mise install` to install the pinned Python, uv, and Vale
tools from `mise.toml`. **End users do not need mise.** After installation,
run `slopvac doctor` to check the Vale prerequisite.
Install slopvac for persistent use with uv:

Upgrade the installation with `uv tool upgrade slopvac`. To run slopvac without
a persistent install, use `uvx slopvac README.md`. uvx reuses its cached
environment. Use `uvx slopvac@latest README.md` to force the latest release.

`init` creates `slopvac.toml` with the `normal` profile when absent and keeps an
existing config unless you pass `--force`. Replace `README.md` with the file or
directory to check. A passing run exits 0. Findings above a threshold exit 1.
An incomplete check exits 2.

If the cache contains a newer stable PyPI release, Slopvac prints an update notice after an eligible command.
Slopvac refreshes that cache in the background. A newly discovered release can appear on a later run.
Slopvac skips the check in these cases:

- The command is `prime`.
- The output format is non-text.
- The report goes to a file or opens in a browser.
- The environment contains `CI`.
- Standard error is not a terminal.
To disable the check, set one of these environment variables:

- `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER=1`
- `SLOPVAC_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1`
- `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`

`--fix` edits source files using deterministic replacements. Before keeping those edits, review the diff. The **[CLI reference](packages/slopvac-lint/README.md)**
covers [linting and fixes](packages/slopvac-lint/README.md#lint-documents),
[profiles](packages/slopvac-lint/README.md#profiles), and
[scoring](packages/slopvac-lint/README.md#scoring).

The linter ships 169 checked rules across 26 categories. The catalog also
carries 69 judgment rules that lint never reports. The
[writing guidance](#writing-guidance) and [semantic review](#semantic-review)
apply them.

The [rule reference](packages/slopvac-lint/docs/rules.md) lists individual rules
and examples. Inspect them from the CLI:

The native engine and Vale report findings with source locations. The report
includes density per 100 words and a 0-100 score. Profiles and project settings
control which findings fail a run.

Missing or unsupported Vale, or `--no-vale`, leaves selected Vale-backed checks unchecked.
Native findings remain available, but the run returns exit 2.

Slopvac installs small project-local files instead of harness marketplaces.
The managed steering block tells the agent to run `slopvac prime`.
Harnesses that load project skills also receive `slopvac-prose`.
That skill directs agents to run `slopvac prime write` and `slopvac prime review` around prose work. Neither
copies rule policy. The installed CLI prints it.
Two commands write these files:

- `slopvac init` creates `slopvac.toml` when absent and keeps an existing file
  unless you pass `--force`. Repeat `--harness <name>` to select multiple harnesses.
  Without `--harness`, it writes generic `AGENTS.md` steering. Naming a harness
  replaces that default, so add `--harness agents` to keep it. `--no-skills`
  writes steering without skills. `--skip-agents` writes only the config and
  rejects `--harness` and `--no-skills`.
- `slopvac setup <harness>` writes, checks, or removes one harness's steering
  and its skill when available. It writes only those files. It reads
  `[guidance]` from `slopvac.toml` and falls back to the defaults if `slopvac.toml` is absent.
  Run it with or without `init`.

`slopvac setup --list` prints each harness with its steering and skill paths.
The [CLI reference](packages/slopvac-lint/README.md#agent-steering) lists the
per-harness paths, `setup --check` exit codes, and `--remove` behavior.
Agents get detailed guidance on demand:

`prime` covers linting, exit-code semantics, Vale coverage, rule explanation,
named exceptions, factual-claim verification, and writing, review, and reporting
guidance. `slopvac prime report` prints an approval-gated issue workflow and
posts nothing until the user approves the exact post.
`slopvac onboard` prints a short setup handoff that points the agent to `prime`.

`slopvac prime write` prints a writing guide for READMEs, docs, PR or MR
descriptions, commit and release text, and specifications. The guide provides a genre table and a documentation contract.
It also gives the `slopvac rules` command for the genre's judgment rules. `slopvac prime` tells the
agent to run it before drafting or editing that prose.

Disable it with `[guidance] write = "off"` in `slopvac.toml`. The
[semantic guidance reference](packages/slopvac-lint/docs/semantic-guidance.md)
lists every mode.

`slopvac prime review` prints a review workflow. The agent runs `slopvac lint`
first, answers the judgment checklist for the document's genre, and checks
factual claims against the code. The default reviewer pass uses one fresh-context subagent.
 The reviewer receives the text and the review output.
For a revision, it also receives the original. It receives the source or brief when available.
The reviewer runs lint and applies the checklist. It verifies factual claims against the source.
Its report names each rule and quotes the affected text, with a proposed rewrite.
It also identifies lost facts and claims stronger than the source. The author fixes or
rebuts each finding. No loop follows unless requested.

For a pass by the author, set `[guidance] review_depth = "self"`.
For repeated reviewer rounds, set `review_depth = "adversary"`. Each round gets the findings the
author rebutted earlier, and the loop stops when a round reports no finding the
author accepts. If no subagent is available, the author runs the pass and
records `self (no subagent available)`. `review = "ask"` asks before the review.
`review = "off"` disables it. Slopvac only prints the workflow and the
checklist. The agent's own model runs the review.

The hook runs the `slopvac` binary on your `PATH`. Set the style in `slopvac.toml`; the 3.0 CLI has no `--profile` or `--style` option. Setup for prek, lefthook, and hk is in [docs/hooks.md](docs/hooks.md).
Add these steps to a workflow job:
Pin the action to a full commit SHA and keep the version as a trailing comment.

The action supports annotations and SARIF output, plus configuration and
changed-file selection. See [action.yml](action.yml) for its inputs and outputs.

The default profile is `normal`. Use `strict` for reference material or
`relaxed` for informal text. Configure thresholds and rule severities in
`slopvac.toml`, with `[[overrides]]` for path-specific settings.

The [configuration reference](packages/slopvac-lint/README.md#configuration)
includes precedence and examples. See
[suppressions and exclusions](packages/slopvac-lint/docs/suppressions.md) for a
local exception or an excluded file, and
[comment mode](packages/slopvac-lint/README.md#comment-mode) for source files.

A passing run means the selected checks stayed within configured thresholds.
It does not establish factual correctness or make an overall judgment about
writing quality beyond the configured rules. AI-signal labels describe rule
evidence without changing the gate.

Before merging a release PR, maintainers can run the report-only local
[performance comparison](packages/slopvac-lint/docs/performance.md#pre-release-regression-comparison)
on an idle host. It reports regressions and exits 0. Set `PERF_FAIL=1` to fail
on them.

Lint is deterministic, and the [semantic review](#semantic-review) is a
checklist that an agent applies. A separate development track evaluates optional **typed judge models** for semantic decisions. Candidate backends include
hosted [Jev](https://www.typesafeai.org/jev) and local/open models such as
[Laya](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya),
[Nimble](https://github.com/bespokelabsai/nimble), and
[Kev](https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev), plus the
[SemIf](https://github.com/theoleecj/semif) direct-logit scoring approach.
The design appears in
[issue #162](https://github.com/slopvac/slopvac/issues/162).
The proposed layer would run **after** Slopvac parses the document and generates candidate spans. It has two uses:

1. **Semantic detection.** For AI/style defects that cannot be expressed
   reliably as syntax, structure, or fixed patterns, a typed judge evaluates
   bounded questions such as applicability, semantic fit, evidence sufficiency,
   and repair category. Slopvac code, not the model, derives the final
   confirm/reject/uncertain policy.
2. **Rule validation.** The provider receives a finding's rule id, exact source span, and local context.
   It assesses whether the trigger matches the intended defect.
   These assessments would measure false positives and validate rule changes against gold/control corpora.
   They would also identify deterministic triggers to improve.

An optional local reranker may sit before the typed judge when candidate volume
is high. The first candidate is
[Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B).
It can prioritize likely candidates to reduce judge cost, but the typed judge
and deterministic host policy remain authoritative.
The intended shape is:
Exact source locations remain host-authoritative. The semantic layer remains separate from the current linter CLI and its exit status.

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for development and pull request guidance. Use [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) to report vulnerabilities in private. File bugs, rule findings, and proposals with an [issue form](https://github.com/slopvac/slopvac/issues/new/choose). Do not post security reports as issues.

Apache-2.0. Includes rules derived from
[hardikpandya/stop-slop](https://github.com/hardikpandya/stop-slop) (MIT).
See [sources](packages/slopvac-lint/README.md#sources) for rule provenance.
Install the pinned development tools and project dependencies from the repository root:
`mise.toml` pins Python, uv, Vale, and other development tools. The project supports Python 3.11 or later. Vale 3.18 or later enables complete linting. Run `mise install` to install pinned tools.
Run the test suite from the repository root:

Run it through `mise exec --` so `vale` resolves to the version pinned in `mise.toml`. Tests marked `vale` run only when a `vale` is on `PATH`. If the `vale` on `PATH` is not the pin (for example a Homebrew install), the run stops with a usage error. CI installs the same pin.

The root `pyproject.toml` configures pytest to discover `packages/slopvac-lint/tests` and `tests`. CI runs the full suite with `python -m pytest` from the repository root. For documentation changes, CI runs the Slopvac prose gate and Markdown checks.

The 3.0 engine is a Cargo workspace under `crates/`. It sits beside the Python package, which stays the reference implementation. `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the toolchain, `mise.toml` pins the same version so a global mise `rust` setting does not override it, and `mise install` adds cargo-nextest. Run these from the repository root:

A new crate needs a `Cargo.lock` entry in `extra-files` in `release-please-config.json`, or the release PR does not bump its version. After you add or remove a crate, run `just sync-release-please` (or `python3 scripts/sync_release_please_crates.py`) to rewrite those entries. The quick-lint CI job runs the same script with `--check` and fails on drift.
Run Slopvac's repository prose gate on the files you changed:

This builds the 3.x binary from your checkout and applies the root `slopvac.toml`. The `prose` job in `lint.yml` runs the same binary. Exit 1 means a finding failed the gate. Exit 2 means the run was incomplete or the invocation was invalid, for example a `slopvac.toml` with no `schema_version`. Exit 2 is not clean, and the `prose` job fails on it. Fix the cause and rerun. Fix findings before you open a pull request.

CI also posts prose and shellcheck findings as review comments on added lines. The lint jobs in `lint.yml` run with read-only permissions and upload their findings as `reviewdog-*` artifacts. Then `reviewdog.yml` runs on `workflow_run` from the default branch, with `pull-requests: write`. It runs without any pull request code, so it works the same for pull requests from forks.

That workflow treats the artifacts as untrusted. It accepts a pull request number only when that PR is open and its head commit is the one the CI run tested. `workflow_run` workflows load from the default branch, so changes to `reviewdog.yml` take effect only after merge. The pass or fail result of the lint jobs does not depend on this path.
Requirements for every Rust change, and the checklist reviewers use, are in [`docs/engineering.md`](docs/engineering.md).

Rust test conventions are in [`docs/testing-rust.md`](docs/testing-rust.md). Install the snapshot reviewer with `cargo binstall cargo-insta` (or `cargo install cargo-insta --locked`) before you change a snapshot.

Rust CI runs rustfmt, clippy, rustdoc, nextest and doctests. A supply-chain job runs `cargo deny` for licences, bans and sources, `cargo shear` for unused dependencies, `cargo sort` for manifest order and `typos`. Advisories run nightly and report on pull requests without blocking them. `mise install` pins the tools. `prek run --all-files` runs the same checks locally.

A separate workflow, `tag-roots.yml`, runs after pushes to main and weekly, and fails when any remote tag points at a commit outside this repository's history. To catch a stray tag before it leaves your machine, run `prek install -t pre-push`. The hook then refuses any push while a local tag has a different root commit, and it lists those tags by full ref name. Remove each listed tag by hand with `git update-ref --no-deref -d <ref>`, using the full ref name as listed, which works for symbolic tags and for names that start with a hyphen.

Licences: `deny.toml` allows permissive licences only. The CC BY-SA 4.0 part-of-speech model covers the model file, so add a per-crate exception for the crate that embeds it. Never add CC BY-SA to the global allow list.

Rule definitions live in [`packages/slopvac-lint/src/slopvac/rules/`](packages/slopvac-lint/src/slopvac/rules/). Each YAML file defines a category and its rules. Add examples of text the rule should flag and text it should leave alone.
Run the ruleset tests after changing examples:

These tests check that each lexical rule's `bad` example matches its pattern. A `good` example must not match. The tests check that each lexical rule has an example. For substitutions, the tests check that each example resolves to a replacement.

Merge the release PR. Then run `just release X.Y.Z` to start publishing from
the matching `vX.Y.Z` tag. For 3.0.0 and later, the recipe starts
`publish-pypi.yml`, which publishes the binary wheels once a passed candidate
has tested the same tree. Earlier versions start `publish-lint.yml`. Either
workflow waits for approval in the `pypi` environment before it publishes to
PyPI.

For 2.x, release candidates build from each update to the release PR branch.
They also wait for `pypi` approval. They get no tag or changelog entry.
For 3.x, you cut a candidate by pushing an `rc/vX.Y.Z-rc.N` tag. See [release candidates](docs/release/candidates.md).
Plain installs and `slopvac@latest` stay on the latest stable release. The package README lists how to opt in to a candidate.

Contributions to slopvac need a signed [Contributor License Agreement](CLA.md) (CLA). It is the Individual Contributor Non-Exclusive License Agreement from the Contributor Agreements 1.2 templates (Harmony), with the traditional patent license. You keep the copyright in your contribution. You grant Sjors Robroek a non-exclusive license to use, sublicense and distribute it, and a patent license.
In return, Sjors Robroek takes on two duties:

- License your contribution under licenses that the Free Software Foundation classifies as free and the Open Source Initiative approves.
- Offer material under a free and open license too, when it also has a license that is not free or not open.
The project stays under Apache-2.0. The laws of the Netherlands govern the agreement.
Contributors sign through [CLA Assistant](https://cla-assistant.io). On your first pull request, the CLA Assistant bot posts a comment with a link. Sign at that link with your GitHub account.
You sign once for each version of the agreement. If the text changes, CLA Assistant asks you to sign again.
The `license/cla` check covers one account for each commit:

- The linked GitHub account of the commit author.
- The linked GitHub account of the committer, when the author has no linked account.
Each such account must sign. `Co-authored-by` trailers are not read, so a co-author named only in a trailer is not checked.
The text that you sign is in the [slopvac CLA Gist](https://gist.github.com/srobroek/5374c748726c6ec555de263ba96c15b4). [`CLA.md`](CLA.md) in this repository is the same text.

If you created the contribution as part of your job, your employer must approve the agreement first. The "How to use this Contributor Agreement" section of the CLA says so. The project has no entity agreement yet. If your employer needs one, open an issue.
Bot accounts that the maintainer allowlists in CLA Assistant don't sign.

Use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/). Release-please reads the commit message to prepare releases. Examples: `feat(rules): add a rule`, `fix: correct a rule`, and `docs: clarify setup`.
Open a pull request with a concise description and a list of checks you ran. CI must pass before merge. Maintainers squash-merge pull requests.
Choose an issue form at [New issue](https://github.com/slopvac/slopvac/issues/new/choose):
The forms cover these categories:

- Bug: covers crashes, tracebacks, wrong exit codes, wrong or unstable output, or config, setup, init, Vale, cache, or prime defects.
- False positive: covers text that a rule flags as slop incorrectly.
- Missed slop: covers slop that no finding reports but an existing rule should catch. Use this form if unsure.
- Mis-tagged: covers a finding on slop with the wrong rule, severity, or span/location.
- Wrong fix: covers a correct match with a wrong message, replacement, or fix guidance. Use this form if `--fix` changes meaning or produces broken text.
- New rule: covers a writing pattern that no existing rule detects.
- Rule improvement: covers whole-rule changes to accuracy, examples, exceptions, judgment, tier, severity, genre advice, wording, or docs.
Before submitting an agent report, run `slopvac prime report`. Get the user's approval for the exact post.

Do not include paths, file names, or private data.
Do not include user names, host names, repository names, or organisation names.
Paste sample text into the report. A local file path is not enough.
Prefer a synthetic sample over text from private or proprietary sources.

Record the agent product name. Record the active model exactly as the harness reports it in its system prompt, context, or `/model` selection. Do not use model self-description or config defaults. Write N/A when the active model is unavailable.
Get the harness version from its version command. Write N/A when unavailable.
Do not infer these fields from environment variables.

Status: approved direction, 2026-11-14. Beads epic `slopvac-8l4`, labelled `slopvac-3.0`, tracks the work.
This document records the decisions, the evidence behind them, and the order of work.
slopvac 3.0 is a Rust rewrite with a public data and plugin API. It also absorbs the fixes that were meant for 2.x, because no further 2.x release ships.

- GitHub issues #252 to #257 from the Mecatl documentation trial, and the open dependency PRs.
- A Slack thread with the same reporter: trial results, model evaluations, and integration feedback.
- Experiments run on 2026-11-14. Their outputs stay out of the repository. The closed evidence beads in the table below record each method and result.
Labels in these experiments are single-annotator, and several samples are small. Treat the figures as estimates for these corpora.
No 2.18.x or 2.19 release ships. The epic "Fixes rolled into 3.0" holds the fixes.
**Rule-data fixes in the Python reference.** These land on `main` without a release. The golden suite then records the fixed behavior, and the rule YAML carries into 3.0.

- #257 title case: count only words that start with one capital, then lower case. Skip acronyms, CamelCase, and project terms.
- #255: split "no longer" into its own rule that fires before change verbs only.
- #254: skip headings and table cells, and require an imperative opener.
- `negative-inventory-core`: fire on inventory forms only, and add the `requirement` exception.
- #256: accept the `versioned-change-note` exception.
- Bound the `future-tense` lookbehind. Hoist shared boundaries in the substitution and token pattern builders.
**Fixes the Rust beads own.** The 2.x beads for these are superseded by 3.0 beads that carry each requirement:

- #253 symlinks outside lint targets.
- #252: the `judgement` checklist honors config, error text keeps every interpolated value, and `prime write` reflects config.
- Update notices reach agents.
- `--format rdjsonl`.
- A warning for `[[overrides]]` globs that match nothing.
- STE stays out of the default behavior.
- release-please covers the Cargo workspace.
**Repository hygiene, to do now.**

- Renovate for version and security updates, with Dependabot raising alerts only (decision 28 in [0001](0001-slopvac-3-architecture.md) supersedes the earlier Dependabot-only plan). Once the CI gate passes, Renovate auto-merges minor, patch and digest updates.
- Triage the open PRs. Close #245, #246, and #191 without merging: 3.0 removes Vale and ships a Rust binary.
- Adopt reviewdog in this repository, with a read-only lint job and a separate reporting job. Until 3.0 adds rdjsonl, reviewdog reads the 2.x SARIF output.

Python-only work is closed as not needed. That covers the standard-library swaps, Vale 3.27 support, and Python 3.15 classifiers.
When 3.0 ships, a bead tracks the replies on #252 to #257 and the Slack thread.

- **Language:** Rust, in a Cargo workspace. The Python 2.x code is the reference implementation until the golden suite passes.
- **Concurrency:** no async runtime. rayon handles CPU work. Dedicated threads handle waiting work. crossbeam-channel connects them, and `select!` with deadlines handles timeouts. ureq handles HTTP.
- **Engine:** slopvac matches every rule itself, and Vale is removed entirely. The README keeps an "Inspired by Vale" section that thanks the project.
pydantic models defined the 2.x schema. In 3.0, Rust types generate the JSON Schema, which is published per API major version.

- **IDs:** namespaced as `<plugin>:<id>`. Built-ins live in `core`. Short names still work where they are unambiguous.
- **Rules:**
  - A typed `match:` block (`tokens`, `pattern`, `substitution`, `metric`, `structure`, `capitalization`, `vocabulary`, `judgement`).
  - Fields for `exclude_blocks`, `contexts`, `applies_to`, and named exception detectors.
  - Test cases in the `vale test` style: `input`, `want`, `contains`, `absent`.
  - `tiers` is removed.
- **Profiles:** set gate thresholds and a severity shift only.
- **Styles:** ordered presets with `extends` and declared `conflicts`. The last listed style wins.
- **Genres:** data files with detection signals. A content type such as `how-to` is a genre that extends a genre. Diátaxis types are consumer content types.
- **Context tags:** `{kind, span, confidence, evidence}` from registered taggers. Taggers are declarative in data plugins and code in plugins.
- **Terms:** `.slopvac/terms.toml`. Each term needs only `term`. `variants` and `kind` are optional.
- **Config:**
  - `slopvac.toml` with `schema_version = 3`, `extends`, `styles`, `plugins`, `[[genres]]`, `[frontmatter]` policy, `[vale]` removed, `[guidance] level`, `[thresholds]`, and `[[overrides]]`.
  - The nearest config to each file applies.
  - Front matter is an allowed-fields layer under a `slopvac:` key.
- **Lint JSON v3:** `schema_version`, `notices`, per-document `genre` and config sources, and per-finding `pack`, `contexts`, and `end_line`.
- **Output formats:** `text`, `json`, `sarif`, `rdjsonl`, `codeclimate`, `junit`, `checkstyle`, `markdown`, `html`, and LSP diagnostics. Each rule has a stable documentation page that the formats link to.

From lowest priority to highest: core defaults, styles, the genre chain, `extends`, project config, matching `[[genres]]` and `[[overrides]]`, front matter, inline directives, CLI flags.
`--explain-config` prints the layer, the file, and the line for each value, and what the value overrode.

- **Data plugins** hold rules, styles, genres, terms, declarative taggers, and prime snippets. They contain no code. A `slopvac-plugin.toml` manifest declares `slopvac_api`.
- **Code plugins** speak JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio. Framing follows LSP. The `initialize` handshake exchanges capabilities. A Python SDK ships with them, and a conformance suite tests them.
  - Hook points: taggers, extractors, reporters, harness recipes, fixers, scorers, and model providers.
  - Python plugins run in their own environment.
- **Distribution:** OCI artifacts on GHCR or any registry is the primary channel. Release archives, local folders, and git pinned to a commit also work.
- **Lockfile:** `.slopvac/plugins.lock` records the version, source, and digest.
- **Signatures:** minisign signatures ship as manifest layers. Publisher keys are listed in the index.
- **Trust:**
  - The plugin host refuses to load an untrusted code plugin. slopvac lists each one with the command that trusts it.
  - `slopvac plugins trust` records trust per content hash. Trust is an explicit command, not a prompt.
  - Agents and CI never trust on the user's behalf.
- **Commands:** `plugins sync`, `outdated`, `update`, `status`, `trust`, and `search`, which reads an index that a job rebuilds automatically. `plugins new`, `validate`, `test`, and `publish` complete the set.

- **prime:**
  - The base topic is about 250 words. It has one line per command and an index of topics.
  - Each topic is a terse checklist with its own index.
  - slopvac renders each topic from a Markdown file, against the config, at the detail that `[guidance] level` selects.
  - `.slopvac/PRIME.md` adds project notes after a topic, labelled as untrusted data. The built-in text always comes first.
- **Setup:** `setup <harness>` supports `opencode`. The flags select the block, the skill, and the reviewer agent, and set the reviewer model. Skills follow the Agent Skills specification.
- **Review:**
  - Types are `mechanical`, `update`, and `rewrite`.
  - Fact checking covers changed claims only, with a scope that scales with the change. slopvac asks the user to confirm the scope when it would be exceeded.
  - Fact preservation uses lexical alignment and a literal diff.
  - The reviewer must use a different model from the author.
- **Model guidance:** prime and the docs list model recommendations per review type. The eval results generate the list.

- cargo-dist builds release archives, installers, and a Homebrew tap (`slopvac/homebrew-tap`).
- maturin wheels keep `uvx slopvac` as the documented default.
- Platforms: macOS (arm64, x86_64) and Linux (arm64 and x86_64 glibc, x86_64 musl). Decided 2026-11-16: 3.0 has no native Windows build. Windows users run the Linux build under WSL, and native Windows is a 3.x feature (decision 26 of the architecture record). This supersedes the earlier Windows target and PowerShell installer.
- Release candidates are `rc/vX.Y.Z-rc.N` tags cut on demand, with a provenance gate before stable. In 2.x, candidates build from each update to the release PR branch, wait for approval in the `pypi` environment, and get no tag or changelog entry.

- `slopvac self update` runs for installs made by our installer. Other installs print the matching upgrade command.
- The GitHub Action uses reviewdog with `reporter: auto`, or uploads SARIF. Its own annotation code is removed.
- MegaLinter and Trunk descriptors follow the release.

- Tests: nextest, `cargo test --doc`, insta, and snapbox or trycmd.
- Lints: clippy with workspace lints, and rustfmt.
- Hygiene: cargo-deny, cargo-shear, typos, cargo-sort, Swatinem/rust-cache, and Renovate for cargo.
- Hooks: prek.
- Added later: cargo-llvm-cov, cargo-mutants on the diff, fuzzing of parsers, CodeQL, gungraun benchmarks, and an MSRV check.
slopvac generates every reference document from code and data, and CI fails when a generated file is stale:

- API schemas from the Rust types: lint JSON, config, front matter, plugin manifest, rules, styles, genres, terms, lockfile, and plugin protocol messages. Each schema is versioned per API major and published at a stable URL.
- One page per rule, with examples, exceptions, contexts, severity per profile and style, and provenance. Output formats link to these pages.
- One page per style preset and per genre or content type.
- The plugin protocol reference, the hook points, the plugin manifest reference, and a page per plugin.
- Rust API docs: crate docs in every `lib.rs`, `missing_docs` on library crates, rustdoc with warnings denied, and docs.rs for published crates.

- `uvx slopvac@latest prime migrate` runs the chain of migrations from the detected version.
- `docs/migrate-2-to-3.md` and `prime migrate` render from one source.
- `slopvac migrate` previews the changes, then rewrites the config with comments kept. It updates directive IDs and steering blocks. It compares findings before and after migration.
- 3.0 has no 2.x compatibility mode. It rejects a 2.x config with exit 2 and points to `slopvac migrate`. Removed flags, options, and hooks fail with an error, with no warning period.
An adversarial review of this plan and its beads found these gaps. Each one now has a bead:

- **Compatibility:** a generated matrix of every 2.x command, flag, and behavior, with a disposition (preserve, migrate, or remove) and an owning bead. Installed-binary tests cover the preserved rows. stdin, `--diff-working-tree`, `--fix`, `reference`, `onboard`, `init`, `setup --remove`, and the published pre-commit hook IDs each have their own bead.
- **Golden suite modes:** reference parity pinned to a Python commit, Vale 3.24, and corpus hashes; 3.0 default-policy tests with reviewed deltas; and migration-preservation tests. The 2.x profiles have per-rule dispositions, so a separate bead maps them onto the 3.0 model.
- **Plugin security:** a threat model and an independent review before the plugin host and OCI client close. The review covers what the signature covers, publisher-key authority, key rotation, extraction limits, subprocess containment, and regex resource limits.
- **PCRE2 build policy:** pin version 10.43 or later, test JIT and non-JIT across macOS, glibc, and musl, and prove a match-limit mechanism.
- **POS tagger:** `harper-brill` failed its spike (`slopvac-8l4.3.10`): noun agreement 3.8% and 10.9% of words untagged. A Rust port of the `prose` tagger passed, with 99.1% exact tag match. Only the opt-in vocabulary blocklist check depends on POS. The binary embeds the model under CC BY-SA 4.0 with attribution and a share-alike notice for the model file only; the code keeps the project licence (`slopvac-8l4.3.23`).
- **Accuracy gate:** recall on seeded and adjudicated positives, false-positive rates on clean controls, and a held-out set, as well as precision.
- **Position contract:** byte spans, line and column bases, and per-format conversions, including LSP UTF-16. Agree these before fixes and suggestions ship.
- **RST:** stays in core through a bundled docutils adapter. AsciiDoc is new and experimental.
- **Performance:** budgets for the installed binary, measured before they gate releases.
- **Policies:** network and privacy, accessibility, and API lifecycle. Breaking changes happen at major versions, with no deprecation windows.
- **Release readiness:** one gate bead that the stable release depends on, separate from building candidates.
- **Interim status:** no 2.x release ships, so the issues get status and workarounds now.

Slopvac 2.x is a Python package. It generates Vale configuration, runs Vale, and scores the output. That design has three limits:

- Matching is split. 2.x has native rule types in Python, and Vale runs the rest. Slopvac filters Vale findings and supplies their metadata, suppression, severity, replacements, and provenance. Each new match type, provenance field, or context tag must work in both engines.
- An ordinary Vale-enabled lint run starts a Python process and a Vale subprocess. `prime` does not call Vale, and `--no-vale` or a disabled config skips it.
- Users install two tools, and the Vale version affects results.

A documentation trial (GitHub issue range [#252](https://github.com/slopvac/slopvac/issues/252) to [#257](https://github.com/slopvac/slopvac/issues/257)) also found rule defects that need fixes. No 2.x release ships, so those fixes and a public data and plugin API land together in 3.0.0.
Labels in the experiments below come from one annotator, and some samples are small (40 to 92 documents). Treat the figures as estimates for those corpora.

- Slopvac owns matching, config, and output, so findings can carry provenance, spans, and contexts.
- One self-contained binary with no runtime to install, and `uvx slopvac` must keep working.
- A small dependency and binary footprint.
- A plugin boundary that a third party can use without running inside the slopvac process.
- Install and update without prompts, so agents and CI behave like people.
- Reference material must not drift from the code.
Rewrite slopvac in Rust as a Cargo workspace. The Python 2.x code stays the reference implementation until the golden suite passes.

- Evidence: the regex spike (`slopvac-8l4.2.15`) ran PCRE2 with JIT at 1.7 to 1.8 seconds on one thread and 0.2 seconds on 14 threads, against 7.7 to 9.1 seconds for Python. This measures matcher throughput for 143 patterns over 8,496 texts. It does not measure whole-run time.
- Rejected: keep Python and Vale. It keeps all three limits above.
Slopvac matches every rule itself. The README keeps an "Inspired by Vale" section that thanks the project.

- Evidence: the PCRE2 spike matched Python on 142 of 143 patterns (decision 4), which shows regex rule patterns run without Vale's engine. Part-of-speech rules are covered by decision 25: only the opt-in vocabulary blocklist check depends on POS tags.
- Rejected: keep Vale as an optional engine. It would keep two code paths and two behaviors to test.
Use rayon for CPU work. Use dedicated threads for waiting work, joined by crossbeam-channel, with `select!` and deadlines for timeouts. Use ureq for HTTP. Write the OCI client by hand.
- Evidence (`slopvac-8l4.2.17`):

- The ureq client did the anonymous token flow and pulled manifests and blobs with sha256 checks from `ghcr.io`. Push was tested on a local registry only, because GHCR push needs `write:packages`.
- Rejected: tokio with `oci-client` (three times the size, 180 dependencies).
- Rejected: smol, which saved 23 lines but added 40 dependencies, and HTTP stayed blocking.

- Evidence (`slopvac-8l4.2.15`): 143 compiled patterns over 8,496 texts. After two `\u` and `\U` escapes were rewritten, PCRE2 with JIT matched Python on 142 patterns with 0 mismatches. `prose-craft.future-tense` failed on an unbounded lookbehind. `fancy-regex` compiled 143 patterns, with 1 backtrack-limit error after hoisting.
- Untested: `$` before a trailing newline, exotic case folding, and unusual `\s` whitespace.
- Rejected: `fancy-regex`, for the backtrack-limit error.
- Rejected: the `regex` crate alone, because it lacks lookaround. It stays optional for patterns that need none.
- Follow-up: bound the `future-tense` lookbehind. Pin PCRE2 10.43 or later and test JIT and non-JIT builds.

- Evidence (`slopvac-8l4.2.16`): 40 excerpts of 22 sentences, three rewrite replicates, and paired bootstrap over documents.
  - Dropped-fact F1: lexical 0.943, 0.915, 0.802 against model2vec 0.798, 0.733, 0.702. The difference of 0.10 to 0.18 is significant.
  - Claim grouping ARI: 0.300 against 0.194, significant.

- Rejected: model2vec. It scored lower on this corpus, so 3.0 ships lexical similarity only. A model2vec plugin is on the backlog.

Markdown uses `pulldown-cmark` and MDX uses `markdown-rs`. HTML uses `html5ever`, and code comments use a pure-Rust lexer. RST stays in core through a docutils-to-HTML adapter. - Evidence: none from a spike. AsciiDoc is new, so it ships as experimental.

- Code comments: the default is a pure-Rust lexer that ports the 2.x comment projection. It tracks block comments and strings in one pass, so a comment marker inside a string is not a comment. It links no C code.
- Tree-sitter: it reads a language only when the grammar has no external scanner. Four grammars qualify: C, Go, Java and Proto. The binary carries no other grammar.
- Reason: a scanner is hand-written C that keeps its own state in raw memory. Review found hangs and memory corruption in the F#, Kotlin and Swift scanners on hostile input. The Dart scanner also crashed on a multi-byte character at a read edge. Rust safety rules and parse budgets cannot contain C code.
- Checks: the lexer is linear. The crate has a fuzz target, and a test fails if a linked grammar gains a scanner.
- Rejected: tree-sitter with every grammar. It added 60 MiB to a release binary and put unaudited C scanners on the path of every source file.
- Cost: Elixir and Julia docstrings are strings, as in 2.x, so the lexer does not extract them. A scanner-free parser for them can come later. Python is the exception: the lexer extracts the string that opens a module, class or function body.

Decided 2026-11-16. 3.0 lints text inside Office and OpenDocument containers and inside PNG images that embed a diagram source. Formats: `docx`, `pptx`, `xlsx` and their macro and template variants (read-only), `odt`, `odp`, `ods`, and draw.io, Excalidraw and PlantUML PNG. EPUB and PDF are out of scope, as are Mermaid, tldraw and Inkscape images and encrypted files.

- Engine: `Engine::lint_binary` takes `BinaryInput { path, bytes, format }`. Text input stays `&str`.
- Extraction contract: a new plugin hook kind, `binary-extractor/extract`, sends bytes inline as base64. First-party extractors use the same contract in process, and wire conformance tests run them too. One validator separates valid-empty, no-source, unsupported, malformed and over-budget. Unsupported content inside a supported input is an `info` notice with exit 0, and the run stays complete. A malformed payload exits 2.
- Positions: segment-local coordinates drive matching, contexts, exclusions and fingerprints. The container byte range is provenance only. `Finding.origin` is an optional structure that carries the locator, label, segment id and local range.
- Fix: `--fix` skips binary hosts with `SkipReason::BinaryHost`.
- Limits: 256 MiB input, ZIP entry-count, size and ratio caps checked before expensive work, DTD off, and bounded PNG chunks. A breach exits 2.
- Approved tradeoffs: in-process first-party extractors, PNG discovery only for `.drawio.png`, `.excalidraw.png` and explicit includes, no binary stdin, macro and template variants included, and xlsx and ods kept with a cell-occurrence model.
- Evidence: a crate survey (`zip` has no read-side bomb guards; `roxmltree` can disable the DTD) and an adversarial review whose revisions are all adopted. No spike measured extraction speed. The PlantUML PNG value encoding is unverified.
- Rejected: bundled subprocess plugins for first-party formats (a spawn plus base64 per file, in return for crash and memory isolation and host-enforced deadlines that the in-process extractors give up), sniffing every PNG, and a container byte offset as the finding position.
- Tracking: epic `slopvac-8l4.20`, bead `slopvac-8l4.2.31`. Detail: [Binary container inputs](binary-inputs.md).

  `common`, `lint-report`, `rule`, `category`, `config`, `frontmatter`,
  `plugin-manifest`, `style`, `genre`, `tagger`, `blocklist`, `terms`, `plugins-lock`,

"Must" is a requirement on the 3.0 binary. "Network" means any connection outside the local machine, including DNS lookups and registry or API calls.

1. `lint`, `validate`, `rules`, `explain`, `prime`, `reference`, and `claims` read local files only. The one exception is the background update check (section 1.2), which the opt-outs in section 1.3 disable.
2. Every network feature is a named command or hook in the table in section 1.2. No other code path opens a connection.
3. Document text, finding text, file paths, and rule hit counts stay local. The update-check request is the only usage-like traffic, and it carries no document data. Slopvac has no telemetry.
4. A failed or refused connection never changes a lint verdict. It prints an error, and it exits 2 (incomplete) only when the user asked for the network operation.
5. Slopvac has no prompts, so consent is an explicit command or flag. A flag such as `--yes` binds a command and cannot tell who ran it. The prime text therefore tells agents to get the user's approval of the previewed output first.

Offline is sticky. If any source sets it, no other source can unset it, and no flag turns it off. This departs from the layer order of the plan, where a higher layer overrides a lower one.
In offline mode:

- A command that needs the network exits 2 with the code `offline-network-needed` and the message `offline: <command> needs the network`. It does not retry or fall back.
- Plugins that the lockfile pins and that sit in the local cache load normally.
- A plugin missing from the cache exits 2 with the code `offline-plugin-missing`. The message names the plugin and the digest.
- `plugins sync` succeeds from the cache alone. It verifies digests against `.slopvac/plugins.lock` and reports each missing plugin.
- `plugins search` opens no connection and reads the index caches only. An index with no cache gets `offline-network-needed` and the run exits 2, with no results at all when no selected index has a cache ([plugin-index.md](plugin-index.md), section 9).

Two features need consent beyond installing slopvac: issue submission and model-provider hooks.
**Issue submission.**

- `slopvac report` prints the exact title and body it would file, then exits. Filing needs `--gh --yes`.
- The body omits local paths, file names, user names, host names, repository names, and organization names. The body includes document text only when the user passes `--include-text <file>`, and the preview shows that text.
- Environment fields come from the CLI, never from environment variables, as `CONTRIBUTING.md` requires for agent reports.
- `slopvac report <category> --title TEXT --field ID=VALUE ...` builds the report from the issue form of that category. The field ids are the form ids, and a missing required field exits 2 with the code `report-incomplete`. Document text comes only from `--include-text FILE`, which reads a regular UTF-8 file of at most 256 KiB.
- Every field goes through a scrub before the preview: the working directory, the home directory, the user name and the host name, path-shaped words (Unix, drive and UNC paths, and relative paths), file names, repository and organization names on GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket URLs (the slopvac repository stays), GitHub tokens (also when a line break splits one), the value of every `Authorization` header, `Bearer`, `Basic`, `Token` and `Digest` credentials and URL user-info. Percent-escapes in a repository URL are decoded before the check, and only a URL host, a leading host or an scp-style `git@host:` counts as a forge address. Document text gets the exact-string and secret steps only, so the sample stays intact.
- `--body-file FILE` writes the previewed body to `FILE`. The name `-` is refused with `report-body-file`, because `gh` reads it as standard input; `./-` names a file. The write goes to a temporary file in the same directory and then renames over `FILE`, so a reader never sees half a body.
- `--gh` requires `--body-file` and prints the command `gh issue create -R github.com/slopvac/slopvac --title TITLE --body-file FILE`, with each word quoted for a POSIX shell. `gh` has no title-file option, so the title is a quoted argument. The host and repository are constants in the binary. No flag or config key changes them, and slopvac clears `GH_HOST` and `GH_REPO` from the environment of `gh`. A body path that is not UTF-8, or that holds a control character, cannot be printed in the command, so `--gh` exits 2 with `report-body-file`.
- `--gh --yes` runs that command after the preview. Slopvac finds `gh` by a plain lookup in the directories of `PATH`, so a `gh` earlier on `PATH` wins; the threat model records this as a residual risk. It starts `gh` with an argument list and no shell. It first runs `gh auth status --hostname github.com`. When `gh` is missing, the command exits 2 with `report-gh-missing`. When the login check fails, it exits 2 with `report-gh-not-logged-in`. When `gh issue create` fails or runs longer than 60 seconds, it exits 2 with `report-gh-failed`. Slopvac never reads, stores or logs a token, and it prints none of the output of `gh` except the issue URL. Offline mode makes `--gh --yes` exit 2 with `offline-network-needed` before anything is written or printed. `--gh` alone is offline-safe.
- Without `--gh`, the command is offline-safe and prints a prefilled issue-form URL. `--open` starts the browser, except in offline mode, where the URL is only printed.
- The preview shows the target, the title and the body, and no labels, because `gh issue create` would not apply them. The prefilled-form path prints the labels the issue form sets (the category label and `needs-triage`). The form never sets `agent-reported`, so the command never promises it.
- `report` reads no token and no secret from the environment. The scrub works on the supplied text and on the working directory, home directory, user name and host name only.
- A control character other than a tab or a newline in the title, a field or the document sample is refused with `report-invalid` (a CRLF pair becomes a newline first). Text with an escape sequence could otherwise act on the terminal that shows the preview. The error does not echo the text.
- An unknown `--field` id is not echoed back.
- The scrub is best effort and never refuses a report. After it runs, a check over the title, each field, the document sample and the body looks for text that may still hold a credential or private data. For each hit it prints a warning on stderr that names only the field and the kind (``warning: possible credential in field `steps`: review it before posting``), never the matched text. The check looks for a GitHub token prefix (also when whitespace splits it), a long mixed letter-and-digit run, an `Authorization` line (also when folded), `Basic`, `Bearer`, `Token` or `Digest` followed by a credential, a forge address other than `slopvac/slopvac` (after decoding escapes, ignoring a trailing dot in the host and resolving `..`), an absolute path, and the working directory, home directory, user name and host name. It also checks the text as typed, before the scrub, because a partial scrub can leave a fragment. Placeholders such as `<token>` and ordinary prose such as `Basic authentication.` draw no warning. The warning does not stop the run, so the reader of the preview decides.
- A usage error for `report` (a bad category or argument) does not echo what was typed.
- The URL carries the title and every answer that fits in 7000 bytes, keyed by form id. It carries no labels, because GitHub answers 404 when the reader may not set them, and the form sets them. Checkboxes stay unticked. The preview names any field that did not fit. A title over 200 characters is refused.
- The issue forms in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE` are generated from the field definitions in `crates/slopvac/src/report/fields.rs`. A test regenerates them and fails on any difference.
- 2.x already requires the agent to get the user's approval of the exact post (`guidance.py`, the `prime report` workflow). 3.0 keeps that rule in the prime text and adds the command-level guard above.
**Model-provider hooks.**

- A model provider is a plugin. It stays off until the user runs `slopvac plugins trust` for it and names it in `slopvac.toml` under `[review] provider`.

- During `lint`, every provider stays idle.
- In offline mode no provider call happens, even for a trusted provider.
- The reviewer model should differ from the author model. Slopvac cannot verify this for a provider it does not control. The check compares the model names that the config and the provider report.
  - When slopvac detects the same model, before the call or from the model the provider reports, the review still runs and the plan carries a `review-model-same` notice at level `warning`.
  - A difference between the requested reviewer model and the model the provider reports adds a `review-model-reported-mismatch` notice at level `info`.

**3.0 requirement.** Every entry point that reads text enforces a size cap before it hands the text to a parser, an index or a matcher. An input over its cap is refused whole, and its text never reaches a parser. The run is incomplete and exits 2, and the error or notice carries the stable code from the table.

The span crates index text with 32-bit offsets and size their structures from its length, and they do not cap their input. Their documentation states the 64 MiB limit as a rule for callers. Memory per read stays bounded by the cap plus one byte, because the reader stops at the cap.

A per-file cap does not bound the work of many files, or of a long list in one file. Aggregate budgets bound it, and the same error rules apply: the input is refused whole, the run is incomplete and exits 2. Each refusal carries `data.budget`, the name of the budget that tripped, `data.limit`, the limit in the unit below, and `data.path`, the config file, plugin directory or document at which it tripped, relative to the root, or `<external>/<file name>` outside it. For `rule-entries`, `data.path` is the rule file. The list of `data.budget` values can grow. A message names only that path and the limit. When `slopvac claims` refuses a text over a context budget, `data.path` names the input that tripped it, the original or the revised file, shown by the same rule. With the default `--format json` the output is then the refusal envelope that `lint --format json` writes (schema version 3, no documents, one notice), not the success report of `claims`, and the exit code is 2. With `--format text` only the error line on stderr is written.
How the budgets apply:

- A config file that more than one file extends is read and parsed once. The loader shares that parsed copy between its applications, so the order of settings and their provenance do not change.
- The `extends` counters differ on purpose. Files applied counts every application, and so bounds the merge work. Bytes read counts each read once, and so bounds the I/O. Bytes applied counts every application by size, and so bounds the settings the result holds.
- An extended file whose ancestor is still waiting to apply counts against the file budget. The loader checks the depth of a reused subtree at each place it applies again, and checks every budget before it adds an application.
- An `extends` cycle is not a budget. It keeps `config-extends-cycle`, and the loader checks for a cycle before it checks the depth.
- A rule file reached by more than one name, such as a symlink, loads once under the first name in file-name order, and the file budget counts it once.
- The plugin loader reads and compiles one file at a time.
- The run budgets (`plugin-run-bytes`, `plugin-run-rules`, `plugin-run-pattern-bytes`) sum over every loaded plugin, and the built-in core plugin counts toward them. The byte budgets (`plugin-bytes`, `plugin-run-bytes`) count each plugin's manifest like any other file it supplies. The per-plugin budgets still apply to each plugin on its own.
- Duplicate checks on lists (unique tokens, unique substitution keys, blocks with the same `files`) use hash lookups, so their cost grows linearly with the list and a long list of distinct items is not a quadratic cost.

Code changes that touch a cap record the new value here in the same change. The reader constants live in `slopvac-fs` (`MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES`), `slopvac-config` (`MAX_CONFIG_BYTES`), `slopvac-update` (`MAX_CONFIG_BYTES`), `slopvac-rules` (`MAX_RULE_FILE_BYTES`), `slopvac-styles` (`MAX_STYLE_BYTES`, plus a private cap in house-style detection), `slopvac-plugins` (`MAX_LOCK_BYTES`) and `slopvac-packs` (`MAX_RUN_BYTES`, `MAX_RUN_RULES`, `MAX_RUN_PATTERN_BYTES`, `GLOB_MAX_BYTES`, `GLOB_MAX_DEPTH`, `GLOB_MAX_ALTERNATIVES`; the regex limits are private).

The CLI file and stdin reads enforce their cap and report `document-too-large` with exit 2. The language server and `migrate` document reads, and the `migrate` config read, enforce theirs in a later change. The synced-plugin run budgets, the `provides` glob limits and the manifest byte accounting take effect with the synced-plugin loader. Every other row is enforced. A `fix` refusal for an oversized file carries the code through `Refusal::code`, and a `--diff` scoping read fails with `DiffError::FileTooLarge`. The `lint` command passes `--fix` to the engine, which reports an oversized file with `document-too-large` through `Refusal::code`. It does not yet pass `--diff-base`; when it does, it reports an oversized file with `document-too-large` too.

A capped file read opens the file without blocking and accepts only a regular file. A FIFO, device, socket or directory at the path is refused at once, so a repository entry cannot hang a run. The refusal reports through the entry point's existing read-failure error, such as `input-unreadable` for a document, and not through a new code. Stdin is the exception: it reads a pipe by design.

Every read in the table below reports a refusal as one of the kinds listed. Each such refusal exits 2. The advisory house-style detection read is the exception: it skips a file it cannot read and does not fail (see its row in the cap table).
The refusal kinds are `unsafe-path`, `not-found`, `symlink`, `not-regular`, `multiply-linked`, `io`, `not-utf8` and `too-large`. The list can grow in a later 3.x release.

Reserved for a later 3.x release, and not emitted yet: the codes `rules-file-unreadable` and `style-unreadable` for the cells above with no dedicated code, `terms-file-unreadable` as a possible later name for `terms-io`, and a `data.reason` key on every refusal that carries the kind as one of the strings above. Until they are emitted, consumers branch on the codes in the table.
Output and protocol caps are separate and already hold: plugin frames 16 MiB, reStructuredText converter output 16 MiB, and fixer edits 1 MiB.

It lists the sentences a revision changed or added and the original sentences it dropped, and the schema is `claims`. `slopvac review` prints the review plan, and the schema is `review-plan`. The plan holds the review type and why it was chosen, the change stats, the scope budget, the exact payload a provider receives and the model notices. Once a model provider is installed, a plan from a provider call also holds the provider's report. Until then, a run that needs a provider fails with `review-provider-missing`, or with `offline-network-needed` when it runs offline, and only `--dry-run` and the mechanical type print a plan. Both documents follow section 3.2. A `claims` run with JSON output that stops at the sentence budget prints a lint report that carries the refusal, not a claims report (section 1.9).

**2.x behavior.** `LintReport.schema_version` defaults to 1. The docstring in `report.py` states the rule: it changes only when a key is removed or retyped, and adding a key does not bump it. The report has a separate `version` key for the tool version. `doctor --format json` has its own `schema_version` of 1 (`doctor_report.py`). 2.x config files have no version field, and `extra="forbid"` rejects unknown keys (`config.py`). The 2.x function `update_notice.upgrade_hint` returns an install-method command such as `uv tool upgrade slopvac`, `pipx upgrade slopvac`, or `pip install -U slopvac`.

- `SchemaVersion` is a positive integer. It counts breaking changes to one artifact's shape and has no minor or patch part.
- Every root instance of a versioned artifact carries `schema_version` with the constant 3. Lint JSON jumps from 1 to 3 so that all artifacts share one number at first. The migration guide states this jump. A later breaking change raises only the number of the artifact it affects, so numbers can diverge after 3.0.
- Changes within one `schema_version` are additive only. Section 3.9 describes the check that enforces this.
  - Allowed: a new optional field, a new optional section, and a new value or alternative in a position that the schema marks as extensible.
  - Direction decides how enums and alternatives may grow. `schemas/v3/directions.toml` lists every schema file as `input` (slopvac reads it), `output` (slopvac writes it) or `both`. A `both` file follows the output rule. The classes are: `input` for blocklist, category, config, frontmatter, genre, plugin-manifest, style and tagger; `output` for claims, doctor-report, lint-report, review-plan and rules-output; `both` for common, plugin-index, plugin-protocol, plugins-lock, rule and terms. The plugin index is parsed and written by the plugin code, and the terms file is read and also saved by the terms command. In an input schema a new `enum` value or an appended `anyOf` member is allowed, and so is an appended `oneOf` member only when it is provably disjoint from every earlier member (different `type`, different `const` or `enum` values, or a shared required property with different `const` or `enum` values, where the compared schemas and their parent can only be objects). An appended `oneOf` member that may overlap an earlier one is `narrowing-possible`, because a document that validated can fail `oneOf`. In an output schema it is breaking, unless the same position carries `"x-slopvac-extensible": true`. Marking a position later, and removing the mark, are both visible to consumers. Adding a mark is allowed, removing one is breaking.
  - Output and `both` schemas fail closed. The check reports a change to any constraint keyword unless it can prove that the new effective schema, which is the `$ref` target together with its sibling keywords, accepts no value that the old one rejected. A widened `type`, a dropped `enum` or `const`, a lowered `min*` bound or raised `max*` bound, a dropped `required` entry, a dropped `uniqueItems`, `format`, `multipleOf`, `not` or `dependentRequired` entry, and an `additionalProperties`, `items`, `patternProperties`, `propertyNames` or `contains` restriction that is removed or opened are all breaking there. In an input schema all of these are allowed. The marker excuses only a widened `type` and a widened `enum` or `const`, not a loosened bound or a dropped `required` entry.
  - As a catch-all, the same schemas report `constraint-changed` for any other keyword that the check does not model and that was changed or removed, once the `$ref` target and its siblings are combined. The exempt keywords are the annotations `title`, `description`, `examples`, `default`, `$comment`, `deprecated`, `readOnly` and `writeOnly`. A schema that is `false` accepts nothing, so replacing `false` with anything else (as an `items`, `prefixItems`, `allOf` or other subschema, or a `$ref` target) is `constraint-loosened`. Replacing `false` with anything else (as an `items`, `prefixItems`, `allOf` or other subschema, or a `$ref` target) is `constraint-loosened`. Adding or removing an `if` while a `then` or `else` exists is `if-changed` in every direction, because it changes which branch applies.
  - Two groups are reported conservatively in every direction, input schemas included, with the kind `constraint-changed`. The first is `contains` together with `minContains` and `maxContains`. The check treats them as one group per schema object, so any change to the group is reported: adding, removing or changing any member, directly or through a reference. A bound next to a `$ref` never cancels a `contains` inside the target. The second is the set of applicators in an object that has `unevaluatedItems` or `unevaluatedProperties`. Those keywords react to everything the other applicators evaluate. Any change to `properties`, `patternProperties`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `prefixItems`, `contains`, `allOf`, `anyOf`, `oneOf`, `not`, `if`, `then`, `else`, `dependentSchemas` or `$ref` in such an object is reported, and so is a keyword that appears or disappears. A missing keyword never equals `true` or `{}`, and an `if` without a branch counts. The check does not try to prove such a change harmless.
  - In an input schema, any change that can make a value that was accepted before rejected is breaking. Adding a property to a closed object, one with `unevaluatedProperties` set to `false`, is such a change, whether or not the new property is required. A new name can retarget a `$ref`, a `$dynamicRef` or an anchor, and an `unevaluatedProperties` check can then reject a value it accepted. The change needs an entry in `compat-allow.toml` that the contract owner approves.
  - Known limit: a presence change is not reported when the merged set of keywords already holds the same value. Removing a sibling `contains` or `items` that duplicates the one in the `$ref` target is an example. Acceptance is unchanged there, so the check stays quiet.
  - An output or `both` schema must not reference a definition in an `input` file, because growth in that definition would go unchecked. The check reports such a reference as `input-definition-referenced`. A definition that several schemas share lives in `common.schema.json`.
  - Not allowed: removing or renaming a field, changing a type, tightening a constraint, or giving a field a new meaning.
- A schema's `$id` never changes within a version. The published URL has the form `https://slopvac.github.io/slopvac/schemas/v3/<artifact>.schema.json`.
- `ApiVersion` is a positive integer for the plugin extension API. The first plugin manifest declares `slopvac_api = 1`. It names the host capabilities a plugin needs. `schema_version` names the shape of one file. The two are independent.
- The binary version is independent of both. A release that adds optional fields keeps `schema_version`. `slopvac --version --json` lists the binary version, each supported `schema_version`, and each supported `slopvac_api`.
  - `schema_versions` is an object. Each key is the name of a versioned artifact's schema under `schemas/v3`, without `.schema.json`. Each value lists the `schema_version` numbers the binary reads or writes for that artifact.
  - The artifacts are `blocklist`, `category`, `claims`, `config`, `doctor-report`, `genre`, `lint-report`, `plugins-lock`, `review-plan`, `rules-output`, `style`, `tagger` and `terms`. The list grows when the binary starts to read or write another versioned artifact, such as a plugin manifest, a plugin index or a standalone rule file. Adding a key, or a number to a list, is additive. Removing either is a breaking change. `slopvac --version --json` does not list `claims` and `review-plan` yet. `slopvac-8l4.12.89` adds them.
  - `slopvac_api` is a list of the extension API numbers the binary supports.
  - The same document also carries `name`, `version`, `install_method` and `notices`.
- A config file without `schema_version` is a 2.x config and is rejected (section 3.7). Any other 3.0 artifact without a version is an error.
- A version higher than the binary supports is an error. The message names the file, the version found, and the versions supported. It also prints the upgrade command for the install method, built as `upgrade_hint` builds it in 2.x.

The rule depends on who wrote the file.

Authors who attach their own data to a user-written file put it under a key with the prefix `x-`. Slopvac ignores `x-` keys wherever it forbids unknown keys and never gives one a meaning. Each artifact schema records this rule in its `description`.

The schema marks which output positions can grow. A position is an `enum`, or an `anyOf` or `oneOf` list, that carries `"x-slopvac-extensible": true`. Consumers must tolerate new values and new alternatives there. Any other output enum or alternative list is closed: a new value is a breaking change and needs a new `schema_version`. A marked position is a promise that a minor release may add to it, so a consumer that matches on it needs a fallback for a value it does not know.

The marker is written by the Rust types for generated files (`extend("x-slopvac-extensible" = true)`) and by hand in the files that are not generated yet. Severity, the AI signal scale, notice levels and the genre source stay closed, because gate and score logic depend on exactly those values. Open string patterns such as hook kinds and feature names have no enum to mark: a reader ignores a name it does not know.
Owners: `slopvac-8l4.2.3`, `slopvac-8l4.2.4`, `slopvac-8l4.2.5`, `slopvac-8l4.2.6`.

The plugin protocol follows LSP. The `initialize` request carries the host's `protocolVersion`, its supported hook points, and its feature flags. The response carries the plugin's `protocolVersion`, the hooks the plugin implements, and the features it needs.

- The host picks the highest protocol version that both sides support. With no common version, the host does not load the plugin and prints both version lists.
- The host calls only the hooks that the plugin declared.
- If the host lacks a required feature, the load stops with an error that names the feature. The host skips an optional feature it lacks.
- Both sides ignore unknown capability names (section 3.3).
- A data plugin has no handshake. The host compares `slopvac_api` with the range it supports. It loads the plugin only if the value is in range.
The plugin protocol bead defines the message shapes.
Owners: `slopvac-8l4.2.6`, `slopvac-8l4.9.6`, `slopvac-8l4.9.1`.

**2.x behavior.** The CLI exit codes are 0 (pass), 1 (a gate failed), and 2 (the run was incomplete) (`contract.py`). Exit 2 means the result cannot establish a pass. 2.x messages have no stable codes.

- The exit codes keep their meaning. Slopvac uses no other exit code.
- Exit 2 (incomplete) means slopvac did not read or did not check part of the input: a file refused over a cap or budget, a file that is malformed or unreadable, or content the engine could not extract. Those notices are warnings. A rule that does not apply is not a failed check. In code-comments mode, a rule that is on by default but cannot run on comments is listed in the info notice `comment-rules-not-run`, and the run stays complete. A rule that should have run and did not makes the run incomplete, and its notice is a warning that names the rules in `data.rules`: a rule of a kind or check the engine does not run (`rule-kind-not-implemented`), a capitalization rule in a style the engine does not run (`rule-style-not-implemented`), and in code-comments mode a rule the user enabled by name that cannot run on comments (`comment-rule-named-not-run`). A warning notice that is not about unread or unchecked input, such as `config-unknown-rule`, leaves the run complete.
- Every error and notice has a stable `code`: a lowercase kebab-case string such as `config-unknown-key` or `plugin-api-unsupported`. The code appears in brackets in text output, in JSON `notices` and errors, and in the generated documentation. Until the generated reference ships, the tables in this contract are the list of codes.
- The `report` command uses these codes, and each exits 2: `report-incomplete` (a required form field is missing), `report-body-file` (the `--body-file` path is refused or cannot be written), `report-gh-missing` (`gh` is not found), `report-gh-not-logged-in` (`gh` is not logged in to github.com), `report-gh-failed` (`gh issue create` failed or ran longer than 60 seconds), `report-invalid` (a title, field or sample holds a control character) and `report-sample-unreadable` (the `--include-text` file cannot be read).
- No code is reused, and no code changes meaning. A code that stops occurring stays in the documentation, marked retired.
- The `review` command uses these codes: `review-model-same` (a `warning` notice) and `review-model-reported-mismatch` (an `info` notice), neither of which changes the exit code, and `review-provider-reply-invalid` (an error that exits 2: a provider result that plugin-protocol.md section 5.3 refuses, such as a missing, extra or duplicate item, or an entry without `text` and `model`). `review-same-model` is retired: a reviewer on the author's model no longer stops a review, and the notice `review-model-same` replaces the refusal.
- Registry logins have two codes. Slopvac asks for a login only when a registry demands one.
  - `credential-helper-untrusted`: the credential helper exists only in a directory that is not trusted (section 1.7 paths: relative to the project, or `<external>/<name>`). Slopvac leaves the helper unstarted and sends the request without a login. When the registry allows that, the run continues and the log carries a warning. When the registry demands a login, the operation fails with this code and exits 2. The user tightens the permissions of the directory or signs in with a static `auths` login or the environment variables.
  - `credential-helper-project-unknown`: the caller did not name the project, so no helper starts. The credential constructors take the project, so only a caller that builds the credentials by hand can reach this code, and a user cannot. It is an internal invariant, with the same outcome.
- Plugin protocol errors use the JSON-RPC 2.0 error object. Its numeric `code` follows the JSON-RPC ranges, and `data.slopvac_code` carries the string code. The protocol bead defines the numeric range.
- Extractors share four codes. `extract-unsupported` covers unsupported content inside a supported input, such as a diagram type that no extractor reads. It is an `info` notice at the root of the report and exits 0, because the input is valid. Skipped content counts toward no score or gate, and the report shows that it was skipped. `extract-malformed` and `extract-budget` are `warning` notices in `unchecked` and exit 2, because the result cannot establish a pass. A broken diagram of a type slopvac reads is malformed, and an unknown type in a recognized fence is unsupported. `extract-output-invalid` belongs to first-party extractors. The failed output of a third-party plugin is `plugin-output-invalid`.
- Three cases exit 2 although the input may be valid: a whole input that the user names in a format slopvac does not read (EPUB, PDF), an encrypted or password-protected container, and a file whose name promises source but holds none (`.drawio.png`, `.excalidraw.png`, `.drawio.svg`; the code is `binary-no-source` for a binary file). A plain PNG or SVG with no source is info and exits 0.
- Three document-level `unchecked` entries cover a whole input. Each makes the run exit 2:
  - `input-unreadable`: the reader refused the file or could not read it.
  - `input-not-utf8`: the bytes are not valid UTF-8.
  - `input-unsupported`: no reader handles this input kind. This includes a whole input that the user names in a format slopvac does not read, such as EPUB or PDF. Slopvac has no separate code for binary inputs.
- When one `lint` or gate run holds both an incomplete input and a failed gate, exit 2 wins over exit 1. An incomplete run cannot establish its own result, and the report still lists the failed gates. This rule is for lint and gate results. The case runner orders its exits the other way: it exits 1 when any case fails, otherwise 2 when a check was incomplete, otherwise 0.
- The engine emits these notice codes, each at the level shown. A warning makes the run incomplete and exits 2. An info notice leaves the run complete and exits 0:

- Message text can change in any release. Codes, rule IDs, and exit codes form the interface.
- A `fix` refusal carries its code through `Refusal::code`: `document-too-large`, `fix-outside-root`, `fix-symlink`, `fix-not-regular`, `fix-hardlinked`, `fix-not-owner`, `fix-unsafe-directory`, `fix-group-mismatch`, `fix-acl-present`, `fix-unsupported-platform` and `fix-changed`.

A `fix` that fails for any other reason, such as an I/O error during the write, reports `fix-failed` and exits 2. The write is atomic (section 1.8), so the target keeps its old content. A staged temporary file may remain beside it.
