**Generation.** The files in `schemas/v3/` are generated from the Rust types by the `slopvac-schemas` crate. CI regenerates them and fails on any difference. Edit the Rust types, never the generated files. The conformance corpus under `schemas/v3/conformance/` is hand-written and stays the referee: the Python and Rust implementations must accept and reject it exactly as each `cases.toml` says. Each artifact moves to generation in its own change.

**Pattern dialect.** Published patterns assume ECMA-262 with the `u` flag, as JSON Schema 2020-12 section 6.4 recommends, and a validator without Unicode mode may refuse to compile them, which fails closed.
**Additive-only check.** `scripts/contract/schema_compat.py` compares `schemas/v3/*.schema.json` with a baseline and enforces section 3.2. It fails on these changes:

- a removed file, or a changed `$id`
- a removed property or `$defs` entry, at any depth
- a new `required` entry
- a narrowed `type`, `enum` or `const`
- in an output or `both` schema, a new `enum` value or an appended `anyOf` or `oneOf` member at a position without `x-slopvac-extensible: true` (`enum-widened`, `alternative-added`), a widened `type` or a dropped `enum` or `const` (`type-widened`, `enum-widened`), or a removed marker (`extensible-removed`)
- in an output or `both` schema, any loosened constraint that the check cannot prove harmless (`constraint-loosened`), such as a lowered `min*` bound, a dropped `required` entry or a removed `additionalProperties` restriction
- in an output or `both` schema, a reference into an `input` file (`input-definition-referenced`)
- a raised `min*` bound or a lowered `max*` bound
- a changed `pattern`
- `additionalProperties` that is newly `false`, or newly a narrower schema

It then validates every `valid/` instance of the baseline corpus against the new schema and fails on any rejection. Added optional properties, new `$defs` entries and new files pass, and so do widened enums and appended `anyOf` members in input schemas, appended `oneOf` members in input schemas that the check proves disjoint from every earlier member, and widened enums or appended alternatives at marked positions. One exception applies: a property added to an object that has `unevaluatedProperties` or `unevaluatedItems`, directly or through its `$ref` target, is reported in every direction and needs an entry in `compat-allow.toml`. Each finding prints as `file:json-pointer: kind: old -> new`. The `kind` is a stable kebab-case code. A code is never reused and never changes meaning (see section 3.5 and `docs/engineering.md`). Exit code 0 means compatible, 1 means a breaking finding, and 2 means a usage or read error, which is never a pass.

**Baseline.** Before the first 3.0 release candidate, the baseline is the pull request's merge-base with `origin/main` (`--base <git-ref>`). This catches accidental breaks in each change. At the release candidate, a snapshot is committed under `schemas/v3/baseline/` and replaces the ref (`--baseline-dir`).
**Limits.** The check fails closed where it cannot decide. Each case below needs an allow entry.

- A `$ref` resolves across every file in `schemas/v3`, on both sides. A change to a shared definition is reported against each referrer, as `file:/properties/p/$ref(common.schema.json#/$defs/D)/minLength`. The output-only findings are the exception when the same definition changed on both sides: they are reported once, at the definition, under the direction of the file that holds it, and the referrer is compared only for its sibling keywords. A retarget, and a reference added or removed, are still reported at the referrer, with the siblings counted as part of the effective restriction. A shared definition that an output schema references therefore belongs in an output or `both` file, and a reference into an `input` file is `input-definition-referenced`. A reference that does not resolve is `unverified`. A schema file without a string `$id` is a read error.
- Proving that a recursive schema and its inlined expansion accept the same instances is out of scope. When a reference was added or removed and the same target recurs, the check stops at that point and reports `unverified`. The corpus re-validation is the backstop.
- `allOf`, `anyOf`, `oneOf` and `prefixItems` compare by position. A list that keeps all its members in another order is `list-reordered`. A new `anyOf` or `oneOf`, and an appended `prefixItems` member, are `narrowing-possible`. So is an appended `oneOf` member that the check cannot prove disjoint from every earlier member. The proof uses `type`, `const` or `enum` values, or a shared required property. The last form holds only where the compared schemas and their parent can only be objects. In an output schema an appended `oneOf` member also gets `alternative-added`, and gets `narrowing-possible` only when the check cannot prove it disjoint in that same way. The two differ: `alternative-added` says consumers meet a new variant, and `narrowing-possible` says the member may overlap an old one, so a document that validated can fail `oneOf`. A marker on the `oneOf` covers both for members appended to an existing list. A newly introduced `anyOf` or `oneOf` is always `narrowing-possible`, marked or not, because it adds a constraint.
- A keyword the check does not model is `unverified` when it is added, removed or changed. Only these annotations never count: `description`, `title`, `examples`, `$comment`, `deprecated`, `readOnly` and `writeOnly`. A changed `default` does count, because it changes what consumers see.
- Each added `required` field is its own finding, located by field name, so one allow entry covers one field.
- The check compares `enum` and `const` as JSON values: a Boolean is not a number.
- If the corpus needs a definition that the new schema deleted, the check exits 2.
- A merge-queue entry uses the base commit that the queue built it on as its baseline.

**Allow-file.** `schemas/v3/compat-allow.toml` is the path for a reviewed breaking change. Each `[[allow]]` entry names the `file`, `pointer` and `kind` of one finding, a `reason`, and the reviewer in `approved_by`. Only the entries that the change adds can go stale. An entry that the baseline's allow file already holds approved a change that has landed, so it never counts as stale. It still suppresses a finding that the baseline also has against itself, unchanged, such as a `$ref` that does not resolve on either side. It suppresses nothing else. So an entry keeps passing after its change reaches the base. A different finding at the same pointer, such as a changed reference, needs a new entry and a new review. An added entry that matches a finding suppresses it. An added entry that matches no finding fails the check, so stale entries cannot pile up. `--allow-file` replaces the tree's allow file. The baseline's allow file is always read from the baseline. The file starts empty.

- piped text output without escape codes, forced-terminal color codes, and `--no-color` without color codes: `test_cli.py`.
`NO_COLOR` has no 2.x test, because 2.x ignores the variable (section 2.1).

- `slopvac-8l4.12.6` adds the preview and `--gh --yes` behavior from section 1.5.
- `slopvac-8l4.13.6` is the Action bead. Its description lists reviewdog, SARIF, and CodeClimate, so it needs the `plugins sync` step and the `--offline` lint step from section 1.4.
- `slopvac-8l4.12.4` confirms which commands may start the update check (section 1.2).

This spec defines where a finding or a fix sits in a file. It covers source-byte spans,
line and column numbers, the mapping from extracted prose back to source bytes, and the
conversion to each output format and to LSP. It owns the semantics of three shared
shapes: [`Span`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/Span),
[`LineCol`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/LineCol) and
[`Edit`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/Edit). Bead: slopvac-8l4.2.11.
The words MUST, SHOULD and MAY carry their RFC 2119 meaning.

A **span** is the only stored position. Everything else derives from a span and the
original file bytes:

- **Byte offsets** into the original file are the canonical form. Rules, parsers, fixes and
  the plugin protocol exchange spans.
- **Line and column** are display coordinates. The linter computes them from a span when
  it renders output. No component stores a column as its source of truth.

A producer that has only line and column, such as an external tool that reports a
column, MUST convert to a span before it hands the position to the rest of slopvac.

The source is the byte sequence that the user would see on disk, or the buffer text in
LSP mode. Four rules fix how it is read.

1. **UTF-8 only.** A file that is not valid UTF-8 is an incomplete check (exit 2). The
   linter MUST NOT repair it with replacement characters. A repair changes byte lengths
   and shifts every later offset.
2. **BOM on disk.** A leading `EF BB BF` is part of the bytes, so offsets count it. It is not
   part of any line. A column on line 1 starts at 1 on the first byte after the BOM, in
   every unit. Offset 0 and offset 3 both map to line 1, column 1. SARIF requires this
   independence from the BOM
   ([SARIF 2.1.0 §3.30.2](https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/errata01/os/sarif-v2.1.0-errata01-os-complete.html)).
   LSP counts a received U+FEFF as a character. See the LSP section.
3. **Line terminators** are LF, CRLF and a CR that does not precede LF. CRLF is one
   terminator of two bytes. Nothing else ends a line: VT, FF, NEL (U+0085), U+2028 and
   U+2029 stay inside their line. This matches LSP's end-of-line list (`\n`, `\r\n`, `\r`,
   [LSP 3.17 text documents](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#textDocuments))
   and CommonMark. A file that ends with a terminator has a final empty line. A position
   at the end of such a file is column 1 of the next line.
4. **No newline translation.** Offsets address the bytes as stored. A reader MUST NOT
   convert CRLF to LF before it computes offsets.
An offset is valid when all of these hold:

- It is at least 0 and at most the file length.
- It is not inside the BOM (offsets 1 and 2 of a BOM file).
- It sits on a code point boundary, so it never lands on a UTF-8 continuation byte.
- It does not fall between the CR and LF of one CRLF.

A combining mark is its own code point. An offset between a base letter and its mark is
valid. The contract does not know about grapheme clusters.

A [`Span`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/Span) is `[start, end)` over byte
offsets.

- **End is exclusive.** The byte at `end` is not part of the span.
- `start <= end`, and both are valid offsets. A span with `start == end` is empty and
  marks an insertion point or a position finding.
- A span MAY cross lines. A span that includes a terminator ends at column 1 of the next
  line.
- A span addresses source bytes. A projected range addresses extracted text, and the
  projection mapping converts one to the other.

JSON Schema cannot state `start <= end` or the boundary rules. The schema checks
integer and minimum only, so a consumer MUST validate the rest. The reference converter
and the vectors define the checks.

A [`LineCol`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/LineCol) has a 1-based `line`
and a 1-based `column`.

The **column** counts the code points from the start of the line to the position, plus
one. The count starts after the BOM on line 1. A tab is one column. Nothing expands tabs
or measures display width. A combining mark is one column.

The default unit is the Unicode code point because it is what a person counts in the
source, it needs no encoding choice, and it is the unit that Rust `char` iteration yields.
A format that needs another unit converts from the span. The unit table lists them.

Rules match extracted prose, not source bytes. A Markdown parser drops emphasis markers,
decodes entities and joins soft-wrapped lines, so a match offset in the prose text is not a
source offset. The projection carries the mapping back.

A projection is an ordered list of **tokens**. Each token has projected text and a source
range `[start, end)` in bytes. Projected offsets count code points of the concatenated token
text. Source ranges ascend and never overlap. Gaps between them are source the parser
dropped: markup, tags, delimiters and line terminators.

One exception applies to the table cells of a reStructuredText grid table. The cells read one
by one, and a cell that wraps over several lines can end after the next cell starts in the
source. In the projection of a document, two things then differ from the rule above:

- The text tokens of a table may be out of source order. They still never overlap one
  another.
- The space that stands for the line break inside a wrapped cell is a **bridge**. Its range
  runs from the end of one line of the cell to the start of the next, so it covers the source
  of the cells beside it and can overlap the text tokens of a later cell. The space between
  two cells is a zero-width synthetic bridge at the end of the previous cell. A bridge belongs
  to no extent of the block, so the source it covers is not taken for that block's text.

A projected range maps to the hull of the real tokens it touches: the smallest start and the
largest end, so the span never inverts. A range over only the bridge inside a cell maps to the
bridge's own range. Markdown and HTML tables put no bridge inside a cell, and their cells ascend. Every other projection keeps the full rule: tokens ascend and never overlap. The vector
`table_cells_out_of_order` covers the exception.

All kinds except `wrap` are **real**: they have a non-empty source range. Every projected
point of a non-identity token maps to the whole token range. `wrap` is the only
**synthetic** kind. Parsers MAY add kinds in a minor release, and each new kind MUST say
whether it is real.
To map a projected range `[ps, pe)` to a span:

1. Drop synthetic points from both edges of the range.
2. If real points remain, the span starts at the smallest source start and ends at the
   largest source end among them. Interior synthetic points and dropped bytes fall inside
   the span.
3. If none remain, the span is empty at the source start of the point at `ps`.

An empty range follows rule 3. The point at the end of the text uses the source end of the
last token.
Three consequences follow:

- **A span covers a whole entity, escape or other multi-byte token.** A range that ends inside `fj` widens to the whole entity. - **A match across a soft wrap includes the line terminator.** For `foo⏎bar` a match on `foo bar` spans all seven bytes, or eight with CRLF. A match that ends at the synthetic space ends at the real text before it. - **Markup between matched characters falls inside the span.** A match on `a b` in `a b` spans through the tag.

- **Markdown and MDX.** Entities, backslash escapes and MDX escaped braces, such as `\{`, are
  tokens. A JSX string expression that renders text is `opaque`. Soft wraps are `wrap`.
  Inline code is `masked`.
- **HTML.** Entities are `entity`. Tags and comments are gaps. A run of whitespace, with
  or without newlines, is one `collapse` token.
- **reStructuredText.** The core parses the document with docutils. docutils records the
  source lines of every block and keeps the source text of every inline construct, and the
  core places each node's words inside that node's own lines, never elsewhere in the file.
  Backslash escapes are `backslash`. Emphasis, strong, link and role markers are gaps. RST
  has no HTML entities. An inline literal is `masked`, and the whitespace between words is
  `collapse` when the source has it there. Positions are byte exact for every word that is
  found inside its node. When a node's words cannot be matched, its prose is kept and maps
  to the node's whole trimmed lines (`opaque`), so the position is line-precise, and the
  document carries an `info` notice. A node with no usable source lines makes the check
  incomplete. docutils 0.21 puts the line of some directive output one line late, so the
  mapper retries with one line of slack before it falls back. A table cell is matched only
  inside its own columns, read from the table border, and a table is a block that covers
  its cells and borders. Text docutils generates, such as the title and entries of a
  `contents` directive, is not prose.
- **Code comments.** The delimiters (`//`, `#`, `/*`, `*/`, a leading `*`) are gaps.
  Consecutive comment lines join with `wrap`. Comment text is not decoded.

An [`Edit`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/Edit) addresses source bytes. A fix
for a match inside a decoded token replaces the whole token, because the span covers it.
The `text` is source text and goes into the file verbatim. The rule or the fix generator
escapes it for the host syntax. A fix that cannot be written as source text, such as one
that needs an entity inside a code span, MUST be suppressed instead of emitted.

A binary host is a container, such as a `.docx`, `.pptx` or `.drawio.png`, from which an
extractor returns one or more text segments. The source model above describes text files.
For a binary host it applies to each segment, never to the container bytes.

A **segment** is the UTF-8 text an extractor returned. Its **local coordinates** are byte
offsets into that text, and line and column derive from them by the rules above, with the
segment as the source. The segment text is not a file, so the BOM rule excludes nothing. A
leading U+FEFF is an ordinary character of one column, as in an LSP buffer, and the byte
after it is at column 2. An invalid offset is invalid against the segment text.

- **Matching, contexts, exclusions and fingerprints use local coordinates.** A rule sees the
  segment text and a span in it. Context windows, exclusion ranges and fingerprint inputs
  are computed from the same local span. None of them reads a container offset.
- **The container byte range is physical provenance only.** It says where the segment came
  from in the container, for example the compressed entry in a ZIP. It can be
  larger or smaller than the segment, and it is not a position in the text. Moving a segment
  to another physical range, with the same text, changes the provenance and nothing else.
- **Rendered output is the locator plus the local line and column.** Text output is
  `path!locator:line:col`, with the code-point column from the unit table. The locator names
  the segment inside the container. The text form is normative. The renderer
  percent-encodes `%` as `%25` and `!` as `%21` inside the path and inside the locator, so
  the first `!` always joins them. A locator can contain colons, so a reader takes `line`
  and `col` from the right, splits the rest at the first `!`, and then decodes both parts.
  The rendered line and column are never container offsets, and they never replace the
  locator.
- **SARIF uses `logicalLocations`.** The result location carries the container path as
  `physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri`, percent-encoded as the SARIF report does, with
  no `region`. The locator is `logicalLocations[].fullyQualifiedName`, with kind `resource`
  for a container part and `element` only for an XML element. A SARIF region would claim a
  position in the artifact bytes, which the local line and column are not. The local span
  goes in `location.properties["slopvac/local"]` as a `start` and `end` pair of
  `LineCol`, and `message.text` repeats the text form for people. GitHub code scanning may
  show no line annotation for these alerts, because the location has no region.
- **Binary hosts take no Edit and no fix.** The span addresses segment text, and an `Edit`
  addresses container bytes that the linter cannot rewrite. The linter MUST NOT emit an
  `Edit` for a binary-host finding, and an edit set aimed at one is invalid.

The origin contract (bead slopvac-8l4.2.29) defines the locator grammar and the
`Finding.origin` field that carries it. Neither is defined here.
An edit set belongs to one finding, or to one file for `--fix`. It applies atomically.

- Every span uses the **original** offsets. Order in the array does not shift offsets.
- Sort by `(start, end)`, and keep array order for equal pairs.
- Two edits **overlap** when one starts before the previous edit ends. A zero-width edit
  strictly inside another span overlaps it. Edits that touch at one offset do not overlap.
- Zero-width edits at one offset apply in array order.
- A zero-width edit at the start of a non-empty edit sorts first and does not overlap it.
- An overlapping set is invalid. The linter rejects the whole set and applies none of it.
- Replacement text is written verbatim. A fix MUST NOT rely on CRLF conversion, and it
  keeps the file's terminator style by writing the same bytes it replaced.
- The BOM is outside every edit that starts at or after offset 3, so it survives.
Every format derives from the span and the original bytes. The vectors pin each row.
An empty span renders with equal start and end wherever the format has an end.

[SARIF 2.1.0 §3.14.27](https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/errata01/os/sarif-v2.1.0-errata01-os-complete.html)
requires `columnKind` on a run that has results over text artifacts. It allows
`utf16CodeUnits` and `unicodeCodePoints`. `utf32CodeUnits` is not a legal value.

**Decision: slopvac emits `utf16CodeUnits`.** Both values are valid. A consumer that does
not support the declared kind MUST recompute columns, and an unreliable recompute is
the failure to avoid. GitHub's SARIF support page shows `columnKind` set to `utf16CodeUnits`, and JavaScript-based viewers index strings in UTF-16. Emitting the unit the main
consumers use makes the declared unit and the number agree even when a consumer ignores
`columnKind`. The cost is a conversion from the span for any line that has a supplementary
code point.

`startColumn` and `endColumn` are 1-based. `endColumn` is exclusive: the region does not
include the character at `endColumn` (§3.30.8). A region that includes a line's terminator
ends at column 1 of the next line (§3.30.2), which is what a span does. Emit `endLine` always, so a multi-line
region is not lost. A BOM never changes a column.

A SARIF `fix` replacement uses a text region with the same conversion as the result
location. An insertion has equal start and end.

The reviewdog format defines `Position.column` as a 1-based count of UTF-8 bytes, for
example the column of `b` in `a𐐀b` is 6
([reviewdog.proto](https://github.com/reviewdog/reviewdog/blob/master/proto/rdf/reviewdog.proto)).
The range end is exclusive, and an end of column 1 on the next line includes the line
terminator. A `Suggestion` carries a range and replacement text, so an `Edit` converts
by the same rule. The proto does not mention a BOM. Slopvac counts bytes from the first
byte after the BOM, as in every other unit.

The [Code Climate spec](https://github.com/codeclimate/platform/blob/master/spec/analyzers/SPEC.md#locations)
has line-based and position-based locations. It treats them as alternatives. It says line
ranges are **inclusive** and lines are 1-based. It does not name the column unit of a position
or say whether a position end is inclusive.

**Decision:** emit `location.lines` only. GitLab Code Quality, the main consumer, requires
`lines.begin`, and the unspecified position semantics would not be portable. `lines.begin` is
the start line. `lines.end` is the line of the last included character, so a span that ends at
column 1 of the next line ends on the previous line. An empty span has `end` equal to `begin`.
Columns do not appear in this format.

The JUnit XML schema that Jenkins ships
([junit-10.xsd](https://github.com/jenkinsci/xunit-plugin/blob/master/src/main/resources/org/jenkinsci/plugins/xunit/types/model/xsd/junit-10.xsd))
has no line or column attribute on `testcase`. Put `path:line:col` in the `failure`
message with code-point columns. Do not invent attributes.

A Checkstyle `<error>` has `line` and `column` attributes and no end
([XMLLogger](https://github.com/checkstyle/checkstyle/blob/master/src/main/java/com/puppycrawl/tools/checkstyle/XMLLogger.java)).
Emit the 1-based start with a code-point column. Checkstyle itself expands tabs by its
`tabWidth` setting. Slopvac does not. Consumers treat the column as a character index.

The workflow command takes `file`, `line`, `col`, `endLine` and `endColumn`. The page says
`line` and `col` start at 1, and it describes `endColumn` only as the "end column number"
([GitHub workflow commands](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-commands)).
It does not name the column unit, the `endColumn` base or whether the end is inclusive. Slopvac emits
`line` and `col` only, with a code-point column, as 2.x does.
These render `line:col` for people. They use the same code-point column as text output.

LSP 3.17 negotiates how `Position.character` counts. The client lists
`general.positionEncodings`. The server answers with `positionEncoding`. The kinds are
`utf-8`, `utf-16` and `utf-32`. UTF-16 is the default and every server MUST support it. A
missing list means `['utf-16']`
([initialize](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#initialize),
[Position](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#position)).

**Server choice.** Pick the first of `utf-8`, `utf-32`, `utf-16` that the client offers.
Otherwise answer `utf-16`. UTF-8 needs no conversion because spans are bytes. UTF-32 is
the code point unit of `LineCol`. UTF-16 is the fallback every client handles. An empty
list counts as `['utf-16']`.

`Position.line` and `Position.character` are 0-based, so convert with `line - 1` and
`character - 1` of the unit's column. A `Range` end is exclusive.

**Buffer coordinates.** LSP positions count the text the server received in `didOpen` or
`didChange`, not the file on disk. If that text starts with U+FEFF, the character is part
of line 1 and counts one column in every unit (three in `utf-8`). The disk rule that
excludes the BOM does not apply. So `Hi` after a BOM starts at character 1 in `utf-16`
and `utf-32` and at character 3 in `utf-8`. The server MUST compute LSP ranges from the
buffer text, never from disk columns. Byte offsets in a buffer also include the U+FEFF
bytes. A client that strips the BOM before it sends the buffer sends no U+FEFF, and the
server's offsets are then 3 less than the disk offsets. The server tracks which case it
holds per document.

An offset in a `TextEdit` or diagnostic converts through the negotiated encoding only. The
server MUST re-derive positions from its own copy of the document after each change
notification and MUST NOT cache them across versions.
Line numbers refer to files in `packages/slopvac-lint/src/slopvac/`.

- **No span on findings.** `Finding` has `line`, `column` and `end_column`
  (`model.py:238-254`). It has no end line and no byte offset.
- **Code point columns after newline translation.** The pipeline reads files with
  `Path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")` (`pipeline.py:315`). That call
  translates CRLF and CR to LF and turns invalid bytes into U+FFFD, which changes byte
  lengths. A BOM stays as U+FEFF, so line 1 columns are off by one against the 3.0 rule.
- **Projection.** `ProjectionMap` maps each projected code point to a raw byte range
  (`projection.py:32-117`). Entities and inline code are emitted with an empty raw range
  (`projection.py:317-322`, `projection.py:301-305`), so the entity's own bytes belong to no
  projected point and `slice_raw` returns nothing for it. `Block.position` turns the raw byte
  offset into line and column by decoding the prefix and counting `\n`
  (`analyze.py:409-422`).
- **Multi-line matches lose their end.** When the end falls on another line, the engine
  sets `end_column` to the end of the start line (`engine.py:878-879`).
- **SARIF declares the wrong unit.** `SarifRun.column_kind` defaults to `utf16CodeUnits`
  and also allows `utf32CodeUnits` (`report.py:249-251`). The values written are code
  points (`report.py:366-370`). `utf32CodeUnits` is not a SARIF value. The region has no
  `endLine` (`report.py:183-188`).
- **Fix offsets disagree with report offsets.** `apply_fixes` splits with
  `str.splitlines(keepends=True)` (`diff_scope.py:413-418`). That also splits on VT, FF,
  FS, GS, RS, NEL, U+2028 and U+2029, while `Block.position` counts only `\n`. A guard that
  compares the matched text (`diff_scope.py:430`) skips a mismatched fix, so the failure
  is a missed fix, not a corrupt one.
- **Vale columns pass through.** Vale findings take their column from Vale's span
  (`vale.py:296-318`) with no check against the source.
- **Formats.** 2.x has text, json, github, sarif and html. Both json and github use
  `finding.column`. rdjsonl, codeclimate, junit, checkstyle and markdown output are new in
  3.0.

- Findings and edits carry a `Span` in original-file bytes. Line and column derive from it.
- Files are read as bytes. Invalid UTF-8 is exit 2 and CRLF is kept.
- The BOM is outside line 1 columns.
- Decoded tokens keep their full source range.
- SARIF emits UTF-16 columns that match `columnKind`, plus `endLine`.
- Fixes use the same line table as reports, and CR and CRLF are terminators everywhere.
- Multi-line findings keep their end line.

The 2.x JSON `line` and `column` fields do not carry over. 3.0 invalidates 2.x outputs at
release, and `slopvac migrate` is the only bridge for configuration.

[`schemas/v3/conformance/positions/vectors.json`](../../schemas/v3/conformance/positions/vectors.json)
holds language-neutral vectors. Documents are JSON strings with `\u` escapes, so the file
survives editors that normalize text. The sections are:

- `positions`: offset to line and column in `utf8`, `utf16` and `utf32`.
- `invalid_offsets`: offsets that MUST be rejected.
- `spans`: start and end positions per unit, and the payload of every output format except LSP.
- `invalid_spans`: spans that MUST be rejected.
- `edits` and `invalid_edits`: edit sets and their results.
- `projections`: token lists and the span each projected range maps to. A case with `"unordered": true` holds table-cell tokens that are out of source order, and a token with `"bridge": true` in it may overlap the source of the text tokens.
- `lsp_ranges`: LSP ranges per encoding, computed over the received buffer text. They include BOM regression vectors.
- `lsp_negotiation`: client offers and the encoding the server picks.
- `binary_hosts` and `binary_host_invalid_spans`: segment-local positions, physical
  provenance, the rendered text and the SARIF location of binary-host findings.

The documents cover ASCII, emoji, a ZWJ family sequence, supplementary-plane letters, combining marks, CJK, tabs,
CRLF, a lone CR, a BOM, characters that are not terminators, a final newline and an empty
file. The projection cases cover entities, escapes, escaped MDX, soft wraps, collapsed
whitespace, skipped tags, RST emphasis, comment lines and masked code.

The Python reference is
[`tests/contract/position_reference.py`](../../tests/contract/position_reference.py). The
test is `tests/contract/test_positions.py`. The Rust port reads the same file and MUST pass
every case. A projection vector tests the mapping algorithm and token rules. A parser's own
tests must show that it emits those tokens for real input.

`slopvac lint --format json` writes one report that validates against
[`schemas/v3/lint-report.schema.json`](../../schemas/v3/lint-report.schema.json). The
bead is slopvac-8l4.2.2. This page states what the schema cannot: where each 2.x key
went, and the rules a consumer relies on. Field descriptions live in the schema.

- `schema_version` is 3. Lint JSON jumps from 1 to 3, so no report carries 2.
- Consumers must branch on `notices[].code` and `unchecked[].code`, never on the message
  text. A code keeps its meaning for the whole 3.x line. Codes are kebab-case.
- Extractors share four codes: `extract-unsupported`, `extract-malformed`, `extract-budget`
  and `extract-output-invalid`. Unsupported content inside a supported input, such as a
  Mermaid `gitGraph` block or a PlantUML mind map, is a root `notices` entry with the code
  `extract-unsupported` and level `info`. The run stays complete and exits 0. Malformed
  content (`extract-malformed`) and content over a limit (`extract-budget`) are `unchecked`
  entries at level `warning`. They make the run incomplete and exit 2.
- An unknown diagram type in a recognized fence, such as `gitGraph` or `@startmindmap`, is
  unsupported. A broken diagram of a type slopvac reads, such as an unclosed `@startuml`
  block or Mermaid front matter that never closes, is `extract-malformed`.
- Content that slopvac skips counts toward no score and no gate. The report shows that it
  was skipped, through the `extract-unsupported` notice.
- Three cases exit 2 although the input may be valid. A whole input that the user names in a
  format slopvac does not read, such as EPUB or PDF, is an error. An encrypted or
  password-protected container is an error. A file whose name promises source but holds
  none, such as `.drawio.png`, `.excalidraw.png` or `.drawio.svg`, is `binary-no-source` for
  a binary file and `extract-malformed` with the reason `no diagram source` for a
  diagram file. A plain PNG or SVG with no source is not an error. It is info and exits 0.
- `extract-output-invalid` belongs to first-party extractors only. The result of a failed
  third-party plugin is `plugin-output-invalid`.
- `slopvac_version` names the tool build. It does not signal a schema change.
- Binary extraction adds root notices. Skipped content inside a binary document is an
  `info` notice `extract-unsupported`, never an `unchecked` entry, and it does not change the
  exit code. Every output format carries it, and the language server shows it as an
  Information diagnostic. [plugin-protocol.md section 5.5.4](plugin-protocol.md#554-outcomes)
  defines it and the other binary codes.
- The schema is strict, because it is the producer contract. Slopvac writes only reports
  that validate, and its own tests check that. A consumer must ignore unknown fields, as
  [the field policy](policies.md) requires, so a later 3.x release can add keys. Keys that
  start with `x-` are reserved for extensions and have no meaning.
- Minor releases add keys and codes only. A removal or a type change waits for 4.0.
- `line`, `column`, `end_line` and `end_column` are the display position. `span` is the
  byte range, from [`Span`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/Span). A finding
  with no source range, such as a document-wide metric, omits `span`, `end_line` and
  `end_column` together.
- `fix.edits` hold [`Edit`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/Edit) values.
  Their byte ranges address the original text and never overlap.
- `gate` is the verdict for one document under its profile. Exit codes still come from
  the run: 0 passes, 1 means that a gate failed, 2 means that the run was incomplete.
These keys have no 2.x counterpart.

- Root: `notices`, replacing `notes`.
- Document: `genre` with its `reasons`, `contexts_seen`, `config_sources`
  ([`ConfigSource`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/ConfigSource)) and `gate`.
- Finding: `pack`, `span`, `end_line`, `contexts`, `fix` and `provenance`
  ([`RuleProvenance`](../../schemas/v3/common.schema.json#/$defs/RuleProvenance)) and
  the optional `origin` (see [Finding origin](#finding-origin)).

A notice may carry `data`, a JSON object whose values may be any JSON value, nested objects and arrays included. A notice with no details
omits it. Each notice code documents its own keys, and a consumer must ignore keys it does not know. For the codes in the tables below that the engine emits, the schema declares the documented keys and their types. For any other code, the schema does not constrain the keys.
These codes list rule ids in `data.rules`, an array of strings in sorted order:

- `rule-kind-not-implemented`
- `rule-style-not-implemented`
- `comment-rules-not-run`
- `comment-rule-named-not-run`
- `cases-rule-unchecked`
`extract-unsupported` has these keys:
`review-model-same` and `review-model-reported-mismatch` locate a model. A notice carries no `path` and no document text. The keys of each code:

An `items` entry has the `role` of the payload item (`changed`, `added`, `dropped`, `original_document` or `revised_document`) and its `line`. The line sits in the revision, except for `dropped` and `original_document`, which sit in the original.
`extract-budget` has these keys:
`data.budget` takes one of these values:

The binary extraction budgets are `segments`, `part`, `locator`, `text` and `in-flight`; the [`BinaryBudget`](../../schemas/v3/plugin-protocol.schema.json#/$defs/BinaryBudget) enum in the plugin protocol schema lists them. A frame overflow is not a budget breach: it is the protocol error `message-too-large`.

The list of budget names can grow in a later 3.x release, so a consumer must handle a
name it does not know. The plugin protocol's error `data` for the same code uses the
same keys.
`config-budget-exceeded` has these keys:

`rules-budget-exceeded` has the same three keys. `data.budget` is `plugin-files`, `plugin-entries`, `plugin-bytes` or `rule-entries`, and `data.limit` is in the unit that policies.md, section 1.9, gives for it. `data.path` is the plugin directory, or for `rule-entries` the rule file, relative to the root, or `<external>/<file name>` outside it.

The budget keys appear wherever the code appears: on a notice, on an `unchecked` entry and on an error. They are not only notice data. The rule loader fills them on its error today, and the report carries them for `config-budget-exceeded`.

`config-unknown-rule` is a `warning` notice. It does not make the run incomplete and does not change its exit status. A config layer named a rule id that no rule has. This covers a rule that 3.0 removed. The notice has one entry for each place that names the id. Its `path` is the config file, relative to the root, or `<external>/<file name>` outside it. A notice whose code this section does not list may still carry `data`. A consumer reads only the keys it knows and ignores the rest.

A container document, such as a Word file or a draw.io diagram, is linted as a list of
extracted text segments. `origin` names the segment that holds a match. It is optional
and absent for plain text files. The bead is slopvac-8l4.2.29.

`range` uses the closed `SegmentRange` shape, not the common `Span`. A `Span` addresses
the original file bytes, and a segment range does not. `SegmentRange` takes no `x-` keys.
`start` is at most `end`, and both fall on code point boundaries of the segment text.
`matched_text` equals the segment text inside `range`.

- `line`, `column`, `end_line` and `end_column` count in the segment text, not in the
  container. They follow the rules in [positions](positions.md) with the segment text as
  the file.
- `span` is optional. When present it is the physical byte range in the container, and
  it can be wider than the match, for example the whole entry when the container
  compresses it. A consumer must not read it as the match. The existing rule still ties
  `span` to `end_line` and `end_column`.
- A finding with an origin carries no `fix`. The schema rejects a finding that has both,
  and the `slopvac-model` type refuses to decode or serialize one. An edit addresses
  container bytes, which the linter cannot rewrite. See
  [Binary hosts](positions.md#binary-hosts).

- A locator is opaque. A consumer compares two locators byte for byte after JSON
  decoding, and treats each as a whole string without parsing, normalizing or case-folding.
- Escaping: these characters are written as `%XX` for each of their UTF-8 bytes, with
  uppercase hex: `%`, controls (U+0000 to U+001F, U+007F to U+009F), U+2028, U+2029 and
  bidirectional overrides (U+202A to U+202E, U+2066 to U+2069). Every other character,
  including `/`, `#`, `[`, `]`, `@` and non-ASCII text, appears as is. A `%` in a locator
  is always the start of a `%XX` escape, so the schema rejects `%zz` and `%0a`.
- Length: at most 3072 code points of the escaped form. A binary extractor sends at most
  1024 characters, and the host checks the two limits in this order: (1) at most 1024
  characters as sent; (2) the escaped length at most 3072, else the document fails with
  `extract-budget` and `data.budget` `locator` (see
  [plugin-protocol.md section 5.5.5](plugin-protocol.md#555-limits)). A percent sign or an
  ASCII control character escapes to 3 characters and U+2028 to 9, so a locator within the first
  limit can still breach the second. A producer that needs more shortens the path by using
  a stable id the format provides, and never truncates.
- Uniqueness: within one document, a `locator` identifies one `segment` and a `segment`
  has one `locator`. Findings in the same segment share both and differ in `range`. Each pair of
  segments has distinct locators and distinct ids. JSON Schema cannot check this across findings, so the
  producer validator of slopvac-8l4.20.1 enforces it, and a consumer may rely on it.
- The `label` holds at most 256 code points, with the same forbidden characters but no
  escaping. A segment id matches `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}(?![\s\S])`.

Take the same container bytes, the same extractor and the same `schema_version`. A
document then yields the same segments, with the same locators, segment ids and ranges,
on every run and platform and in any order of work.

A producer prefers an id that the format stores, such as a Word `w14:paraId`, over a
position. The locator grammar of a format is frozen for the whole 3.x line. A change
waits for 4.0.

A locator can differ between two versions of the container. An example is a paragraph
inserted before a position-based locator.

[positions.md](positions.md#binary-hosts) is the authority for the rendered forms. A SARIF
result for a finding with an origin gets:

- `locations[0].physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri` for the container file, with no
  `region`. A region would claim a position in the artifact bytes, and the segment-local
  line and column are not one.
- `locations[0].logicalLocations[0].fullyQualifiedName` set to the escaped `locator`,
  and `name` set to `label`. Its `kind` is `resource` for a container part and `element`
  only for an XML element.
- `locations[0].properties["slopvac/local"]` holding the local start and end as a pair
  of `LineCol` values under `start` and `end`, plus `"unit": "code-point"` and
  `"base": 1`. Lines and columns are 1-based, and the column counts Unicode code points
  from the segment line start, as in [positions](positions.md#binary-hosts). They are not
  UTF-16 code units, whatever `columnKind` a SARIF region would use.
- `message.text` repeating the text form `path!locator:line:col`. The renderer encodes
  `%` as `%25` and `!` as `%21` in the path and in the locator. A reader takes `line` and
  `col` from the right, splits the rest at the first `!`, then decodes both parts.

The `segment` id and the byte `range` stay in the JSON report. GitHub code scanning can
show no line annotation for these alerts, because the location has no region.

A fingerprint for a finding with an origin hashes the rule id, `locator`, the start and
end of `range`, and the normalized `matched_text`. It leaves out `span` and every position in
the container. Moving a segment inside the container, or recompressing it, keeps the
fingerprint, and editing the segment text before the match changes `range` and the
fingerprint, as it does for plain text. The renderers and fingerprints are slopvac-8l4.20.12.

`contexts` names the text context a match sits in. Comment text in a source file carries
the tag `code-comment`, singular like `prose` and `code-span`. The input mode
`code-comments` is a different thing: it selects the input surface (`--mode`, and a rule's
`applies_to.modes` in [`rule.schema.json`](../../schemas/v3/rule.schema.json)). The mode keeps
its plural spelling because it is a CLI and config value. The two spellings differ on
purpose, and no code maps one to the other.

A 2.x key is `preserve`d, `rename`d or `remove`d. 3.0 has no deprecation window and no
compatibility mode, so a renamed or removed key is gone at release. Run
`tests/contract/test_lint_report_2x_keys.py` to check that this table matches the 2.x
models in `slopvac.report` and `slopvac.model`.

These 2.x readers and writers use the old keys. The 3.0 output beads own the move:
slopvac-8l4.12.2 for the formats.

- The SARIF builder in `report.py`. Owner: slopvac-8l4.12.2.
- `html.py`. Owner: slopvac-8l4.12.2.
- The annotation output in `pipeline.py`. Owner: slopvac-8l4.12.2.

`schemas/v3/conformance/lint-report/` holds the corpus. `valid/multi-document.json` is a
realistic three-document report. Each file under `invalid/` fails at the pointer named in
`cases.toml`. The corpus is the snapshot: schemas generated from the Rust types must
accept and reject the same files.
Status: contract for 3.0. Bead `slopvac-8l4.2.5`. Plan: [slopvac-3.md](../design/slopvac-3.md). Decision: [architecture record 0001](../design/0001-slopvac-3-architecture.md), section 20.

The schemas are [`config.schema.json`](../../schemas/v3/config.schema.json) for `slopvac.toml` and [`frontmatter.schema.json`](../../schemas/v3/frontmatter.schema.json) for the `slopvac:` block. Field meanings live in the schema `description` fields. This document states what the schemas cannot: layer order, merge rules, discovery, and the move from 2.x.
Each statement is a **2.x behavior** with its source in `packages/slopvac-lint/src/slopvac/config.py`, or a **3.0 requirement** with an owning bead.
Lowest priority first. A higher layer wins.
The order comes from the plan, section "Layer order". Environment switches (`SLOPVAC_OFFLINE`) are source `env`. They only set sticky values, so they sit outside the order (section 1.3).

**2.x behavior.** The chain had three layers: the profile, the top-level tables, and each matching `[[overrides]]` block in file order (`config.py`, module docstring and `resolve_for`). Front matter, genres, styles and `extends` did not exist.
**3.0 requirement.** A higher layer patches a lower one field by field.

- A scalar replaces the lower value. This covers `profile` fields and `locale`.
- A map merges by key. This covers `rules`, `categories`, `thresholds` and `terms`. A higher layer that names one key leaves the others alone.
- A list replaces the lower list. This covers `exclude`, `styles`, `terms.allow`, `terms.files`, `terms.blocklists` and `files`. A project that wants the default `exclude` plus one pattern restates the defaults. This matches 2.x, where a user `exclude` replaced the default list (`Config.exclude`) and an override `locale.allow` replaced the project's.
- An explicit threshold survives a profile change. The resolver picks the final profile across all layers. Then it applies each `thresholds` entry on top, layer by layer (`resolve_for`, which also does this in 2.x).
- `severity_shift` moves the levels that come from rule definitions, styles and the genre chain. A level that a `rules` or `categories` entry sets is final, and the shift leaves it alone. `off` stays `off`, and the result clamps at `suggestion` and `error`. The numbers for each built-in profile are in the profile mapping (`slopvac-8l4.2.10`).
- A higher layer cannot reset a field to unset. It sets a value. The one exception is the category budget: `max_per_100_words = "none"` clears a budget that a lower layer set, so a profile override can drop it. 2.x had no spelling for this, and thresholds have none either.

Sticky settings break the rule. `network.offline = true` in any layer, from any file in an `extends` chain, from the `SLOPVAC_OFFLINE` variable or from `--offline`, makes the run offline. No layer can set it back. See [policies.md](policies.md), section 1.3.

Scopes that apply to one file combine in file order, not by specificity. A glob that is more general and later in the file wins over a narrower one earlier. 2.x works this way (`resolve_for`), and 3.0 keeps it because file order needs no ranking of globs.

`guidance`, `network`, `review`, `plugins`, `index`, `styles`, `extends`, `frontmatter`, `mode` and `exclude` apply to the whole run or to file selection. They are not part of the `Settings` patch. An `[[overrides]]` or `[[genres]]` block that names one is an error, and so is a front matter field of that name. 2.x already rejected `guidance` in an override (`Override._reject_guidance`). 3.0 extends the rule to the other tables.

`[[plugins]]` lists every data plugin and code plugin that the project uses, in one array. Each entry has `id`, `source` and an optional `version` requirement. The config does not state the kind: the plugin manifest declares it, and the lockfile records it (plugins.md, section 2).

- Each `id` appears once. A repeated id is an error at the second entry.
- `core` is reserved for the built-in plugin, which the binary compiles in. An entry with the id `core` is an error.
- A listed code plugin starts only after `slopvac plugins trust` records its content hash. A code plugin that is not trusted never starts. The run reports it with the code `plugin-untrusted` and exits 2.
- A separate `[[packs]]` array is an unknown key.

`[index]` sets which indexes `slopvac plugins search` reads (plugin-index.md, sections 5 and 6). It is project-scoped. There is no user-level config layer, and an environment variable, front matter, `[[overrides]]` block, `[[genres]]` block or inline directive cannot set it.

- `default` is a boolean and defaults to `true`. It turns the signed first-party index on or off.
- `[[index.extra]]` is a list of at most 16 extra indexes. The default index does not count. A file with more entries is refused with `config-budget-exceeded`, `data.budget = "index-extra"` and `data.limit = 16`, before the duplicate-name check and before any fetch (policies.md, section 1.9). The loader checks every file, extended files included, and a later layer replaces the list instead of adding to it, so the merged list never holds more than 16. Each entry has `name` and `source`, both required.
- `name` is a lowercase slug of the form of a plugin id: a letter, then letters, digits and hyphens. `core` and `slopvac` are refused, because `slopvac` is the name of the default index. Each `name` appears once. A repeated name is an error at the second entry.
- `source` is an `oci://` reference or an `https://` URL, at most 2048 characters. It carries no user-info. `http://`, `git+https://` and a path are invalid.
- Naming an index grants it no trust (plugin-index.md, section 10).
- A refused `source` is reported with its field, such as `index.extra[0].source`, and the reason: unsupported scheme, user-info, no host, whitespace or too long. The message never repeats the value, because a source can carry a credential (policies.md, section 1.7). Rendered output masks the value of every `index.extra[*].source` in the quoted config line, whichever diagnostic quotes it, keeping the quotes, line and column.
Every resolved value carries a `ConfigSource` (`common.schema.json#/$defs/ConfigSource`):

- `layer` is one of the names in section 1.1, or `env`.
- `file` is the path relative to the project root. A value from a plugin uses `plugin:<id>/<path>`. A `core`, `cli` or `env` value has no file.
- `line` and `column` are one-based and point at the key that set the value. For front matter, they count from the start of the document file, not from the start of the block.
- A `[[genres]]` or `[[overrides]]` value uses layer `override`. The report names the block by its index.

`slopvac lint --explain-config` prints the layer, file, line and column of each value and the value it overrode. 2.x printed only a label such as `overrides[0] (docs/**)` (`provenance` in `resolve_for`). Owners: `slopvac-8l4.4.2` for the stack, `slopvac-8l4.4.7` for diagnostics.
`slopvac lint --explain-config <targets>` prints how the settings of each input resolve, then exits. It lints nothing: no report, no gate and no summary.

- It writes to standard output and exits 0. A target that cannot be read, or a config that cannot be loaded, is reported on standard error as for a lint run, and the exit code is 2.
- It prints one block per input, in argument order, with a blank line between blocks. A block is headed by the input's path as the report shows it (policies.md, section 1.7), or `<stdin>` for standard input.
- Below the heading, a block lists `config root: <root>` and one `config file: <file> (<layer>)` line for each file of the config stack. The root is `.` for the working directory, the path relative to the working directory for a directory below it, and `<external>/<name>` for any other directory (policies.md, section 1.7). The root and the path metadata (the heading, the config files and the origins) never carry an absolute path. Values are printed as configured, except that a value that is a URL is printed without its user-info, query and fragment.
- Every field of the output, the heading included, is escaped as one line, so a file name or a value cannot inject a control sequence or a line break.
- Then comes each resolved key as `<key> = <value>  [<layer> <file>:<line>:<column>]`. The origin of a `core` value has no file. Each value the key replaced follows on an indented line `replaced <value>  [<origin>]`, highest layer first.
- Until front matter takes part in resolution, a block ends with the line `front matter overrides are not shown`.
- The output is text only. `--explain-config` with a `--format` other than `text` fails before any file is read, with the code `explain-config-format-unsupported` and exit 2.
- `--explain-config` with `--min-score`, `--max-per-100-words`, `--locale`, `--category`, `--disable`, `--out`, `--open` or `--verbose` fails the same way, with the code `explain-config-option-unsupported` and exit 2. It does not show the command-line layer yet, and the refusal keeps it from ignoring those options.

**2.x behavior.** `find_config` runs once from the working directory (`cli.py`, `config_path or find_config(Path.cwd())`). It checks `slopvac.toml`, then `.slopvac.toml`, then a `[tool.slopvac]` table in `pyproject.toml`, in each directory from the start upward. It stops after the first directory that contains `.git`. The docstring of `config.py` says discovery walks up from each target file. The code does not: one config applies to every file in the run.

1. For each file, start in the file's directory. Walk up, one directory at a time.
2. The first directory that holds `slopvac.toml` supplies the config. Call it the nearest config.
3. A directory that holds `.git`, as a directory or a file, ends the walk after its own `slopvac.toml` is checked. The walk never leaves the repository.
4. A file without a `slopvac.toml` on its path uses the core defaults.
5. Only the nearest config applies. A parent config does not merge in on its own. Use `extends` to inherit.
6. `--config <path>` skips discovery and applies that one file to every file in the run. Its directory is the root for globs.
7. Input from `--stdin` uses the nearest config of the working directory.
8. A config pattern in `exclude`, `files` or a negated form matches the path relative to the directory of the nearest config. A file outside that directory matches no override. The 2.x fallback to the bare file name is removed.
9. Path values for files (`terms.files`, `terms.blocklists`, a local `plugins` source, `extends`) are relative to the file that holds the value.
10. The walk finds only `slopvac.toml`. A `.slopvac.toml` file or a `[tool.slopvac]` table that the walk meets is a 2.x config and is rejected (section 5).
Resolution is cached per directory, so a run over many files reads each config once.

- Entries apply in list order, and a later entry wins. The extending file wins over all of them.
- An entry is a path relative to the extending file, or `<plugin>:<name>` for a config that a plugin ships.
- An extended file is a v3 config. It must carry `schema_version = 3`. It may extend others.
- A cycle is an error that names the chain: `config-extends-cycle`.
- The nearest config decides `exclude` globs and override globs, wherever the pattern was written.

The block is the mapping under the `slopvac:` key of a document's front matter. Front matter in YAML (`---`), TOML (`+++`) or JSON is read, and the block has the same shape in each. The schema validates the parsed mapping. Conformance instances are YAML.

- `v` is required and equals 3, the same number as `schema_version`. A larger value is an error that names the versions supported and the upgrade command.
- The fields are `genre`, `profile`, `locale`, `thresholds`, `categories`, `rules` and `terms.allow`. No other key is allowed, and a misspelling is an error at its line and column.
- `[frontmatter] allow` in the project config sets which fields take effect. The default is `genre`, `locale` and `terms`. A field outside the list is an error: `config-frontmatter-field-denied`. Slopvac reports it every time.
- The default list lets a document weaken its own gate without a project opt-in, the same way an inline `slopvac-allow` comment does. A document that picks a lenient genre, or lists `terms.allow` words, changes what it is held to. A stricter project removes `genre` from the list. For example, `allow = ["locale", "terms"]` makes a `genre` field in any document an error, and the genre comes from the `[[genres]]` blocks or from detection.
- The `genre` field changes the genre only. Contexts that a `[[genres]]` block or the config assigns to a file are additive, so a document cannot remove them by naming another genre. The report lists both the front matter reason and the path reason.
- `[frontmatter] enabled = false` makes `slopvac:` ordinary data. Slopvac neither reads nor validates it.
- Keys outside `slopvac:` are the document's own and are never checked.
- Keys that start with `x-` are ignored inside the block.

- Every `slopvac.toml` carries `schema_version = 3`. A file without it, or with 2, is a 2.x config.
- Unknown keys are errors with file, line and column, and the nearest valid key. Keys that start with `x-` are ignored. The exception is a map keyed by rule or category name (`rules`, `categories`). Its keys are data, so `x-` has no special meaning there ([policies.md](policies.md), section 3.3).
- A rule or category key is qualified (`<plugin>:<id>`) or a bare name that is unambiguous across the active plugins. An ambiguous name is an error: `ambiguous-category` or `ambiguous-rule`. The same holds for a bare `--category` or `--disable` value. An unknown rule id is the warning notice `config-unknown-rule`. The notice does not make the run incomplete and does not change its exit status ([lint-report.md](lint-report.md), Notice data). An unknown category is an error. The schema checks only the form.
- `rules` takes a bare level. The 2.x table form `[rules."x"] severity = "off"` is not valid, because a level is the only field.
- Two blocks in `[[overrides]]` or `[[genres]]` with the same `files` set are an error: `config-duplicate-scope`. This keeps `Config._reject_duplicate_scopes` from 2.x. The patterns compare as a set after whitespace is trimmed.
- A `[[genres]]` block assigns a genre to the files it matches and patches their settings. The genre itself is defined in a genre file (`genre.schema.json`, owned by another bead).
- Config `exclude` and `files` patterns use gitignore syntax. Slopvac checks the file path first, then its parent directories from nearest to farthest, and stops at the first path or directory that any pattern matches. At that path or directory, the last matching pattern wins. A positive match excludes the file for `exclude` or selects it for `files`. A pattern that starts with `!` does neither. If no pattern matches the file or its parents, the list does not exclude or select the file.
- A threshold absent from a profile and from every layer is unset, and its gate does not run.
3.0 invalidates 2.x configs. No compatibility mode exists, and there is no warning period. Section 3.7 of [policies.md](policies.md) states the policy.

- A config with no `schema_version`, or with 2, makes every command that reads config exit 2 with `config-legacy-version`. The error names the file and points to `slopvac migrate`. Nothing is linted.
- Discovery treats a `.slopvac.toml` file and a `[tool.slopvac]` table as 2.x configs and fails the same way.
- `slopvac migrate` is the only path. It previews every change and then rewrites the file with comments kept. It compares findings before and after.
- A setting with no 3.0 equivalent stops the migration with `config-legacy-dropped`. The error names the key, the file, the line and the reason. `migrate` writes nothing until the user removes or rewrites that setting. It reports every such setting in one run.
Owners for the behavior: `slopvac-8l4.16.1` for `migrate`, `slopvac-8l4.4.5` for the version check.

- **preserve**: the key and its meaning carry over. `migrate` copies the value. For the `exclude` and `files` pattern rows, the key and the patterns carry over, but the files that match can differ, because 3.0 matches as section 4 states.
- **migrate**: 3.0 has the setting under a new key or form. `migrate` rewrites it.
- **remove**: 3.0 has no equivalent. `migrate` fails with `config-legacy-dropped`, except where the table says the removal is lossless or ends in a notice.

Rule and category names change with the plugin model. `migrate` maps a 2.x name such as `prose-format.no-unicode-dash` to its 3.0 qualified id through the rename table in the binary. A name with no entry stops the migration. The exception is a `slopvac-allow` comment that ends on a later line, whatever id it names. 2.x read each directive on one line and rejected that comment. `migrate` leaves it as written, reports `migrate-directive-invalid` as a warning and continues. The table is part of the profile and rule mapping (`slopvac-8l4.2.10`). The rows below call this "rename".
The `minimum_severity` row has one 2.x quirk. `CategorySettings` declares the field twice. The two declarations are identical, so the duplicate has no effect, and `migrate` ignores it.
The conformance corpus is the lasting golden. Generated schemas must accept and reject the same files.

- `schemas/v3/conformance/config/valid/` holds TOML configs: a minimal one, one that uses every table, and one in the shape `migrate` writes.
- `schemas/v3/conformance/config/invalid/` holds one defect per file. Each is mapped to a JSON pointer in `cases.toml`. The cases cover a missing or old `schema_version`, a 2.x `[vale]` table, unknown keys, bad levels, the 2.x table form of a rule and a `guidance` table inside an override. Further cases cover an invalid plugin id, the reserved id `core` and the retired `[[packs]]` array, and an index with a reserved name, an unsupported source scheme or user-info in its source.
- `schemas/v3/conformance/frontmatter/` holds YAML front matter, including a document with other keys, a document with no `slopvac:` key, and an `x-` key inside the block.
- `schemas/v3/conformance/common/` holds `ConfigSource` instances for each layer shape.

A schema checks form only. These behaviors need the resolver and have their own tests there: ambiguous rule names, duplicate scopes, `extends` cycles, denied front matter fields, and sticky offline mode. A repeated plugin id is an error that JSON Schema cannot express, so the config validator checks it and its tests cover it. The same holds for a repeated `[[index.extra]]` name.
3.0 has no 2.x compatibility mode: a 2.x config makes every command that reads config exit 2 with `config-legacy-version`. `slopvac migrate` is the only path.
A config with no `schema_version`, or `schema_version = 2`, needs migrating. `schema_version = 3` is reported as already migrated.
Look for:

- `.slopvac.toml`, or a `slopvac.toml` with no `schema_version = 3`.
- A `[tool.slopvac]` table in `pyproject.toml`.
- `slopvac-allow` comments whose `rule=` value has no plugin prefix, such as `rule=prose-format.no-unicode-dash`.
- Steering blocks between `<!-- slopvac:begin -->` and `<!-- slopvac:end -->` in agent instruction files.

It prints a diff and the finding count of each rule that changed, from the 3.0 engine on your files before and after migration. On the before side, each 2.x config and `slopvac-allow` rule id reads in its 3.0 form. The counts do not come from 2.x and do not show that 2.x results stay the same. It exits 0 and writes nothing.
A 2.x setting with no 3.0 equivalent stops the command with exit 2 and one `config-legacy-dropped` line per setting (file, line, key, reason), and writes nothing.
Causes:

- `[vale]` with `enabled = true`, or with `binary`, `config` or `styles` and no `enabled = false`. Delete the table or set `enabled = false`.
- A rule or category name that is not in the rename table. A `slopvac-allow` comment that ends on a later line does not stop the command, whatever id it names: 2.x rejected it, so migrate leaves it as written and warns `invalid 2.x directive, left as is` (`migrate-directive-invalid`).
- An unknown key, or a `guidance` table inside an override.
Edit and preview again.
A 2.x category with no rules, or a rule that 3.0 removed, is dropped with `migrate-category-removed` or `migrate-rule-removed`. Both exit 0 and point to `removed-rules.toml`.
These also exit 2 and write nothing:

- `document-too-large`: a document is over 64 MiB. Split it.
- `config-too-large`: a config is over 1 MiB. Shorten it.
- `migrate-run-limit`: too many files or bytes. Use a smaller directory.
- `migrate-not-utf8`: a file is not UTF-8. Convert it.
- `config-parse`: a config is not valid TOML. The message gives the line.
- `config-invalid-type`: `schema_version` is not an integer. Fix it.
- `migrate-lint-failed`: the lint could not finish. Fix the file named.
It copies each replaced file to a new backup directory, `.slopvac/migrate-backup/<UTC time>/`, then rewrites it. Config comments and key order stay. It:

- Moves `.slopvac.toml` and `[tool.slopvac]` into `slopvac.toml` and adds `schema_version = 3`.
- Renames categories and rules to 3.0 names. A rule with only a `severity` becomes a bare level.
- Moves `locale.default` to `locale`, `locale.allow` to `terms.allow`, and `vocabulary.path` to `terms.blocklists`.
- Rewrites each TOML blocklist it names: adds `schema_version = 3` and long-form `pos` values (`Noun` to `noun`).
- Deletes a `[vale]` table that has `enabled = false`.
- Qualifies the rule id in each `slopvac-allow` comment, except in code fences and code spans. A comment that ends on a later line stays as written, whatever id it names. A comment for a removed rule on its own line becomes `<!-- -->`, so the paragraphs around it stay apart.
- Replaces each steering block with the 3.0 text.
It stops if one directory holds more than one of `slopvac.toml`, `.slopvac.toml` and `[tool.slopvac]`. Remove the unused ones.
It stops, naming the file and line, for a blocklist that is outside the project, missing, 2.x JSON or YAML, or has a `pos` 2.x rejected.

`--preserve-behavior` keeps the 2.x gates with the `core:legacy-<profile>` style. Each override then needs one pattern, such as `docs/api` or `docs/**`. Others fail with `migrate-override-overlap`. An override that sets a profile takes that profile's levels in its own block.

Before it writes, the command loads each new config as 3.0 does. A config that 3.0 refuses stops it with exit 2 and `migrate-output-invalid`, and nothing is written. It also stops that way when an override sets a profile and a category applies above it. Such a category is set in that override, or in another override whose files meet its files, and a category that 3.0 removed does not count there. Any category named at the top level counts as well, even an empty entry or a category that 3.0 removed. The migrated config could not keep the 2.x levels there.

When the 2.x config sets `vocabulary.path`, `--preserve-behavior` also lists the companion style `core:legacy-<profile>-vocabulary`, so the word blocklist keeps reporting at the 2.x level. Two layouts stop with `migrate-output-invalid`, exit 2 and nothing written: a `vocabulary.path` that only an override sets, and a blocklist together with any profile switch in an override. A follow-up will support these layouts.
Compare `slopvac lint` with the preview report.

To undo a write, run `slopvac migrate --restore`. It uses the backup of the last write, restores backed-up files, removes created files and deletes the backup. It keeps a `.slopvac/` directory you had before. Without `--force`, a file changed since stops it. A write that still has changes to make stops until you restore or remove that backup. To keep the migration, remove the backup directory. A second `slopvac migrate` finds nothing to change.
